#4801. Moving by Numbers: The Trap of the Easily Measurable

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated November 12, 2026 | Reviewed by Abigail Fagan

This post is part of a series. Read part one here.

In the previous post in this series on eating and moving by numbers, we reviewed many years of research (including hundreds of individual studies and over a dozen meta-analyses) on how tracking and quantification affect diet and exercise. And we found that the answer is, on average and in aggregate, “not much”.

In this post, I’ll explore a simple two-pronged hypothesis that’s compatible with that research literature, though not proven by it: that measuring allows you to change 1) only what is easily measurable and 2) only for as long as you keep measuring it.

This idea is sparked by the observation from last time that although none of the results from these meta-analyses of self-monitoring studies are particularly substantial, the biggest, clearest effect is that steps taken seem to increase while step-counting is happening. This raises the possibility that the tracking has more of an effect here because the behaviour of walking is more directly, simply, and meaningfully countable than other kinds of movement are, and a lot more so than eating is. A relatively simple machine can distinguish a step from a non-step, and once it has, then no more human effort is required: you walk, the machine records.

All other kinds of movement are trickier to track than a pace. For example, a recent New York Times article on “Why Weight Lifting Is Good for Your Heart” noted that the constraints and biases of measurement technology are one reason for the persistent sidelining of strength training in research on cardiovascular benefits of exercise: “One of the limitations of studying resistance training—and why it’s taken scientists so long to understand its benefit for the heart—is that exercises like squats and bench presses are hard to track with a wearable device. That means scientists must rely on self-reported data.” It’s frustrating to think just how much mere measurability has helped skew decades’ worth of public health advice towards endurance cardio and away from forms of movement that are increasingly recognised to offer a wider range of benefits.

The difficulty of measuring is even greater with eating than with squatting or cycling or skiing. Because you’re measuring the nutrition ingested rather than the behaviour of ingesting it, a lot more hassle is involved: measuring and weighing amounts of ingredients, calculating energy provision and macronutrient balance, comparing the amount of food prepared versus consumed. The sheer complication of committing to meaningful tracking of one’s eating is one reason why I think its cost/benefit ratio tends to be so poor, in ways I’ll explore in the next part in this series.

So the first step of our inference is that when you use measurement to incentivize change, the changes you end up incentivizing most are not the ones you care most about, the ones that will have the most benefits for anything else in your life—they’re merely the ones you can most easily measure. This leads to a second hypothesis, less directly supported by the existing evidence but certainly not contradicted by it: that these maximally measurable changes may be the least likely to be preserved after the measuring stops.

The formal follow-up data are patchy in general, and they seem to show significant decline across all the habits and “benefits” being studied; after you take away the measurement framework, things seem to revert to baseline at some point between quite slowly and very quickly!

(For example, Vetrovksy et al. (2022), analysing 75 studies, of which 24 included a follow-up phase, found that the step-count increase more than halved in a median of 12 weeks’ follow-up. Chaudhry et al. (2020), analysing 57 studies, report that within two years the increase is down to 10% of the four-month level, and by three to four years people are back to where they started. Freak-Poli et al. (2020), analysing 14 studies, report no change even at short follow-up points.)

Especially given that no other behaviours showed much change to begin with, we can’t confidently conclude anything about how the increases in step count decay relative to changes in other activities. Still, we might speculate that being guided by mere measurability entails a downplaying of other reasons why people might keep doing things: intrinsic rewards like in-the-moment pleasure, good fit with lifestyle and interests and environment, and good fit also with specific health and fitness goals.

Nothing against walking; I just published a personal blog post on what a lovely context it can be for thinking, and it can be delightful in many other ways too. But those delights are, I suspect, mostly not encouraged by the “how many steps have I taken?” lens. When done for counting’s sake, walking may foreground primarily the very quality of monotony that makes it so easy to measure.

A knowledgeable reader (Emily Nicholas Angl) shared an interesting extension of this thought: that immediate “improvements” generated by tracking technologies may have the exact opposite effects over the long term. It’s possible that where counting is strongly emphasised, there’s almost inevitably poor intrinsic drive to maintain the new habit, because the counting has been over-relied on to do all the incentivizing work—and has been applied only to activities that are uncomplicated enough to be readily measured. In this sense, the initial rewards may themselves become the vulnerability.

Looking at this research, it’s instructive to turn our attention to what’s being overshadowed by the quantification. In one paper I included in the review last time (Ferguson et al., 2022), there was a suggestion that quality of life tends to get ignored in the research because it takes longest to change. My intuition as a coach would be the opposite: that if you make changes that are genuinely right for you, greater happiness (or contentment, or purposefulness, etc) is likely to be an almost immediate result—indeed, that intending to enhance everyday experience should be a guide to which changes to make in the first place, because they’re the ones that are likeliest to get embedded and stay there. From this perspective, increasing day-to-day satisfaction is not a nice-to-have that may trickle in eventually, far “downstream” of the solid behavioural changes that really count. Instead, the very experience of having started doing it becomes the reason to keep doing it.

The absence of any mention of participants’ experiences of the changes being measured therefore seems telling in itself: it supports the idea of an overreliance on one ultra-simplistic extrinsic reward (the number) at the expense of any intrinsic rewards, and, in many cases, also of more personally meaningful extrinsic rewards (like specific kinds of ability regained or possibility unlocked). One might extrapolate from here to the benefits that mixed-methods research (including both quantitative measures and qualitative inquiry into participant experiences) could offer to medical research if it turned from an outlier to the norm.

A final dimension I’d like to weave into these speculations about why people do and don’t do the thing we’re asking them to and getting them to measure themselves doing is the question of individual attitude differences. I found myself wondering, as I trawled through the meta-analyses, whether what’s really being assessed in this research is less the cleverness of the tech in getting lazy, greedy humans to be more active and abstemious, but the pre-existing inclination of said humans to be more or less conscientious about the thing they’ve signed up for.

The differences between “compliers” and “non-compliers” (including “defiers”) are well documented as a confounding factor in health research. But I didn’t see any explicit acknowledgement of these dynamics in this literature, despite some studies finding big differences between “high-adherence” and “low-adherence” individuals (the most striking I found being Bertoli et al., 2025, where the former lost an average of 7 kg and the latter 3.5 kg over six months). As a participant, you get out what you put in—but you may not continue to once the study structures are over. And by definition, conscientious compliers won’t keep complying when there’s nothing to comply with! So if all that were driving the changes was conscientious compliance to a tenuous numerical rule, then once the study ends and the rule is lifted, the reasons to continue may seem similarly flimsy.

#4800. Romesh Ranganathan, 48, Lost 44 Pounds by Keeping Fitness Simple—Here's How He Made Exercise Stick

The comedian says strength training, running and consistency—not vanity—have transformed his health.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

Funny and self-deprecating on screen, Romesh Ranganathan takes his health and fitness seriously off it. He's not your typical gym-goer, though. Rather than training to build a bodybuilder's physique or hit performance milestones, his focus is on staying strong, healthy and active as he gets older—and being there for his three sons.

“I got a medical when I turned 40 as I started to worry about my own mortality, not for myself, but because of my kids,” he told On: Yorkshire Magazine. “Before, when I was going to the gym or staying on top of fitness, I'd do it for some sort of vanity reason. I've long since abandoned that and have accepted that I'm never going to look good. So the second half is about my reaction to that medical.”

Now 48, Ranganathan revealed on the Wolf & Owl podcast that he's been training more consistently in recent months. He has previously said he lifts weights three or four times a week—sometimes more if his schedule allows—while also trying to keep his daily step count high.

“I started hitting the gym for weights about three to four times a week, sometimes more if I fancied, and was trying to up my step count and cardio, but my appetite for that is a struggle,” he said in an interview with Huel.

It's an approach that has helped him lose around 44 pounds over the past few years.

Running has also become a key part of his fitness journey. After initially hating it, the comedian went on to complete the London Marathon in both 2024 and 2025.

The turning point came after one piece of simple advice.

“Running is something that people had always recommended to me. But as soon as I had a go at it, I found it unbearable. I'd go out for a run and be blowing after two minutes, then start walking, run a bit more, start blowing again. I'd come back and just feel absolutely battered,” he told Runner's World.

“Then somebody gave me the basic tip of just slowing down a little bit and getting on top of my breathing. That is the single most helpful tip I've ever had; suddenly I went from someone who couldn't face running to seeing all of the benefits of it. That's not to say that it suddenly became easy.”

Ryan is a Senior Writer at Men’s Health UK with a passion for storytelling, health and fitness. Having graduated from Cardiff University in 2020, and later obtaining his NCTJ qualification, Ryan started his career as a Trainee News Writer for sports titles Golf Monthly, Cycling Weekly and Rugby World before progressing to Staff Writer and subsequently Senior Writer with football magazine FourFourTwo.

During his two-and-a-half years there he wrote news stories for the website and features for the magazine, while he also interviewed names such as Les Ferdinand, Ally McCoist, Jamie Redknapp and Antonio Rudiger, among many others. His standout memory, though, came when getting the opportunity to speak to then-Plymouth Argyle manager Steven Schumacher as the club won League One in 2023.

Having grown up a keen footballer and playing for his boyhood side until the age of 16, Ryan got the opportunity to represent Northern Ireland national futsal team eight times, scoring three goals against England, Scotland and Gibraltar. Now past his peak, Ryan prefers to mix weightlifting with running – he achieved a marathon PB of 3:31:49 at Manchester in April 2025, but credits the heat for failing to get below the coveted 3:30 mark…

#4798. The Ultimate Wounded Healer: Remembering Marsha Linehan

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated November 12, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

The mental health community is mourning the loss of Marsha Linehan, the pioneering American psychologist who created dialectical behavior therapy (DBT). Having openly lived with borderline personality disorder—often understood in clinical circles as profound, complex trauma—she embodied the true archetype of the wounded healer. Drawing directly from the depths of her own darkest struggles, she forged a compassionate, life-saving clinical framework that transformed modern psychotherapy and empowered countless individuals to build lives worth living.

Carl Jung first introduced the term “wounded healer” to capture the essence of the archetype embodied by Chiron in Greek Mythology. Jung believed that “disease of the soul” might be the most valuable training for a healer because pain often brings with it profound wisdom and understanding. Through navigating their personal experiences of suffering and adversity, the wounded healer can acquire a profound understanding that suffering, compassion, and the journey toward resilience can only be accessed by living through pain. Within the darkest moments of suffering and despair, unexpected clarity and hidden truths can come to light.

As counterintuitive as it may sound, from tragedy and trauma can come a sacred invitation to grow, evolve, and build wisdom. When hope seems dim, the difficulties you encounter may lead you to a moment of self- examination, an opportunity to look within that may cause you to pause and unravel the lessons hidden within your life’s experiences. Your wounds, rather than simply serving as reminders of past suffering, can transform into wisdom, serving as a compass that directs you toward crafting a life rich in meaning, true fulfillment, and joy. Pain enhances our capacity to empathize and relate to others.

In Greek Myth of Chiron, we find that enduring hardship can serve as a sacred key to personal evolution; it teaches us that amid our deepest emotional suffering lies the golden opportunity to awaken profound resilience and compassion and, most importantly, to illuminate the path to understanding our true purpose in life. A living embodiment of Chiron, Linehan spent 30 years giving severely suicidal patients a reason to live.

Every human experience, from the cradle to the grave, includes some form of suffering or painful and unpredictable life circumstances. Pain is an unavoidable and universal part of being human and requires acknowledgment and understanding instead of being ignored or pushed aside. In the midst of his pain, Chiron found meaning in his ability to heal others, transforming his own suffering into a source of strength that allowed him to connect deeply with those around him. Chiron’s story teaches us that even in the depths of despair, we can find purpose through our suffering. His journey illustrates that personal growth often arises from embracing our pain, learning to heal, and using our experiences to guide and uplift others. This emphasizes the importance of resilience, compassion, and the transformative power of self-acceptance in leading a meaningful life.

Through his tale, we learn that even amid the heaviest darkness, the light of hope can pierce through and offer a pathway to personal growth. Often, the most compassionate and impactful healers are those who have faced their own struggles, as their personal wounds enable them to connect deeply with others who are suffering. May this remind you that even in your own personal suffering, there is potential for growth.

Through my work, I have witnessed the undeniable power that humans have to adapt to, navigate, and even grow from life’s most painful events. When I sit across from a person as they slowly navigate their pain and suffering, I serve as the compassionate witness and guide, eagerly observing the gradual but profound growth that can occur. I believe that the most beautiful thing in the world is seeing the light come into someone’s eyes after they have been lost in the darkness of despair for so long. Witnessing this process feels magical.

Trauma, tragedy, and deep grief all have a way of pushing a person way beyond their comfort zone. It urges you to confront fears and insecurities, but ultimately the journey through pain becomes a sacred teacher, one that illuminates the path to greater self-discovery and awakening. When questioned about his renowned David, the celebrated Renaissance sculptor and poet Michelangelo famously remarked, “I saw the angel in the marble and carved until I set him free.” This insightful quote captures Michelangelo’s conviction that the sculpture lies within the marble block, awaiting revelation through the artist’s craftsmanship. Like Michelangelo, I have focused my life’s work on chiseling away at the unresolved trauma of my clients, cautiously dismantling their defense mechanisms and fears, and gently peeling back the layers of shame to unveil the “authentic self” buried beneath, patiently waiting to be rediscovered and embraced. Within the human psyche exists an innate healing wisdom. As you navigate fears and insecurities, you may uncover a strength you never knew you possessed, a newfound clarity that helps you to transform your pain into purpose, or even a deeper insight that reshapes your struggle into a source of deep meaning. Pain serves as a powerful initiation in the soul’s journey, acting as a catalyst for transformation and growth.

O’Shea Brown, G. (2026). Psyche’s Awakening: A Guide to Emotional and Somatic Healing Through the Wisdom of Greek Myth. HarperCollins.

#4797. Eli teases the launch of a much faster electric microcar

Eli Electric Vehicles is getting ready to reveal a new version of its tiny electric microcar, and this one could expand its usefulness beyond the slow lane.

In an Instagram teaser ahead of EICMA in Milan, the company announced the upcoming Eli ZERO MX, describing it as a new L7e vehicle joining its lineup. Eli also teased a special Race Edition, with promotional artwork showing a dark, sporty-looking ZERO with red accents and a visibly open-sided cabin.

The teaser doesn’t give us much to go on in terms of hard and fast details, but the L7e designation is the biggest clue here.

The familiar European Eli ZERO that we test-drove a few years ago is an L6e light quadricycle, with a top speed of 45 km/h (28 mph). Its compact two-seat layout makes it an appealing urban runabout, though that speed ceiling limits its usefulness on faster roads. But L7e vehicles can typically travel at speeds of up to 80-90 km/h (50-56 mph).

A faster version could make the little EV practical for considerably more trips. And there’s already a tantalizing hint: Eli’s Italian website lists an L7e ZERO capable of 85 km/h (53 mph), with a claimed range of up to 200 km (124 miles). Whether those specifications directly describe the upcoming ZERO MX remains unconfirmed by the teaser.

If they do, that would suggest a much more versatile commuter while retaining the tiny footprint that makes these vehicles so easy to park.

I like the idea of a faster LSV, maybe able to cruise at 40 mph. Not a good idea for freeways but suitable for almost all urban and suburban streets. For some a better option than a bike as an urban or second vehicle.

The Race Edition raises a different set of questions. The new vehicle could feature a sportier design, such as race seats and alternative doors. That could point toward a playful or more tuned vehicle, though we’ll have to wait to learn whether “Race” means additional performance or primarily a styling package.

It’s also unclear how closely the Race Edition and ZERO MX are related. The caption presents them separately, while the artwork additionally points towards a second-generation ZERO.

Either way, a roughly 50 mph Eli would be an interesting proposition: still small enough to rethink how much vehicle a daily commute requires, but potentially fast enough to cover routes the original couldn’t comfortably handle.

Eli says the reveal takes place at EICMA, November 3–8, in Hall 22, Stand B40. We’ll be there to see what they unveil.

IF THERE'S ONE piece of home gym equipment anyone can make room for at home, it's a pair of adjustable dumbbells. Adjustable dumbbells (just like adjustable kettlebells) offer a range of weights from one compact footprint, eliminating the need for multiple sets of weights.

"The Nüobell is the best blend of reliability and authentic dumbbell feel I’ve used," says Samuel, who has been using these for over three years. "The shape and design of these 'bells make them ideal for accessory motions, like skullcrushers and biceps curls, and they’re easy to hold for goblet squats too." Aside from a few scratches, they've held up great to three years of heavy use.

With a maximum weight of 80 pounds of weight per dumbbell and a feel that's nearly indistinguishable from traditional dumbbells, users can utilize the same set of weights for a complete full-body workout. Users can quickly drop down to lower weights for exercises like bent-over flies or pile on the plates for more intense squats. "It features a 'turn-and-click' design rather than just a built-in selector," notes Williams. Users simply turn the handle until they reach their desired weight.

During testing, Howell noted that the Nüobell arrived assembled and was easy to plug-and-play once unboxed. Of all the adjustable dumbbells he tried, these felt the most like actual dumbbells. The major defining features include: metal plates and handles, top-tier construction, easy click-and-go weight adjustment, and the selected weight displayed on the dumbbell itself.

He questioned whether the tempered plastic rack would withstand the constant re-racking of the metal plates over time. Nevertheless, he emphasized that the actual dumbbells are well-crafted and feel solid as hell.

In Howell's opinion, these dumbbells are best for someone who has invested in a home gym and is serious about fitness. They are tailored for the hardcore client who likely has a squat rack and barbell in their garage as well, but wants to add an elite set of adjustable dumbbells to their training arsenal. This weight range suits beginners well, and more experienced lifters can expand the weight by opting for additional expansion kits. For those who find 50 pounds per dumbbell insufficient, PowerBlock offers heavier models such as the Elite USA (up to 90 pounds per dumbbell) or the Pro 100 EXP (up to 100 pounds per dumbbell). Most models of adjustable dumbbells by PowerBlock feature the same pin-and-lock adjustment mechanism, which is easy to use and avoids jamming issues found in some other systems.

In his testing, Howell pointed out the compact structure of the actual dumbbell, noting the plate-like weights, which are more like weighted frames than traditional circular ones. Howell found this design "genius", as the square nature of the dumbbell makes it easy to lay down once done using it without it rolling away or requiring a rack to rest it in. He also appreciated that they arrived assembled and were fairly easy to unpack and begin using.

However, Howell expressed concerns about the durability of certain components, such as the handles and the "clip" that allows you to lock your chosen weight in, which are made of plastic. He believes these dumbbells might not be robust enough for consistent use, particularly for hardcore gymgoers.

Despite these concerns, Samuel praises their adjustability and durability, stating, "I've never encountered a more durable adjustable dumbbell. I love them for farmer’s walks, heavy DB lunges, and thrusters, and rely on them anytime I do a metcon-style workout at home." Samuel also shared he’s dropped these from three or four feet up after tough sets of incline presses, "and they hold up just fine." (Although it's not advisable to make a habit of dropping any adjustable dumbbells regularly.)These dumbbells feature comfortable contoured handles that enhance grip during workouts. However, they do not provide the same weight distribution as traditional dumbbells, as Samuel points out: "If you’re looking to use a set of adjustable movements for plenty of accessory movements, go with something more dumbbell-shaped."

Look for a weight range that meets your fitness goals. Most adjustable dumbbells can be adjusted in 2.5- or 5-pound increments, so it's important to consider a weight range that fits your needs.

Adjustable dumbbells come in different shapes and sizes. Consider the size and shape of the dumbbells and make sure they feel comfortable in your hands. Basically, does the dumbbell feel "good" or natural to you? Again, this comes down to personal preference and might involve some trial and error.

Some adjustable dumbbells distribute the load differently than traditional dumbbells (atypical), changing how it responds to certain movements (particularly accessory movements). A good rule of thumb is if you're looking to perform heavier exercises (farmer's carries, RDLs, rows) you can consider an adjustable dumbbell that doesn't distribute its weight like a traditional dumbbell, such as the PowerBlock option featured above. If you're planning to do more accessory movements (like biceps curls or skull crushers), opt for a traditional dumbbell-shaped option.

There are a few different mechanisms adjustable dumbbells use to switch weights, with some being easier or more user-friendly.

This mechanism uses a dial on the end of the dumbbell handle to adjust the weight. To change the weight, you turn the dial to the desired weight, and the mechanism will lock in the appropriate weight plates. Some adjustable dumbbells must be docked in their storage base to change weight using a dial, while others can be adjusted outside their docking station.

This mechanism uses a pin to select the desired weight and can take some practice to get used to if you're new to it. To change the weight, pull out the pin, select the desired weight, then reinsert the pin into the corresponding slot to lock it in.

This mechanism uses a twist-locking mechanism to secure the weight plates. To change the weight, you twist the handle to unlock the weight plates, remove or add weight plates, and then twist the handle back to lock in the new weight.

Warranties reflect a manufacturer's confidence in its product. And with some of the best adjustable dumbbells priced at or above $500, you want to be sure your investment is protected. So, it’s important to purchase from a manufacturer that offers a clear, comprehensive warranty. They vary widely across the industry, with the most budget-forward brands offering just 90 days on some parts, and others boasting generous five-year warranties on everything. Again, the more you spend upfront, the better the warranty is likely to be. And, if there’s anything that isn’t clear to you about the stated warranty, be sure to ask. It’s your money, after all.

As the Fitness and Reviews Editor at Men's Health, it's my job to test the latest and greatest training equipment, including adjustable dumbbells. To build this guide, I tested more than 30 adjustable dumbbells over the past five years, drawing on my experience and that of my fellow MH fitness editors, including Fitness Director Ebenezer Samuel, C.S.C.S., and Senior Fitness Editor Brett Williams, NASM. Samuel utilized the top-performing adjustable dumbbells featured in this guide in fitness programs with several of his advanced clients.

We also enlisted the help of Maillard Howell of Dean CrossFit in Brooklyn, to test and assess how well these dumbbells performed in the real world (read: a high-traffic training facility). In addition, we sought insights from trainers from both our MH Advisory Board and our Strength in Diversity class for further anecdotal and experiential perspectives on the top adjustable dumbbells.

Each dumbbell was rigorously tested in a variety of categories, including durability, weight distribution, ease of shifting between weights, and aesthetics. All dumbbells were tested with three types of exercises: explosive exercises (such as cleans), multi-joint strength exercises (such as bench presses and Romanian deadlifts), and accessory movements (such as biceps curls and lateral raises). All dumbbells were also dropped from a standard bench to test baseline durability (no adjustable dumbbell should ever be dropped from shoulder height), and they were monitored for signs of rust over a three-month period.

Adjustable dumbbells pack a ton of perks compared to regular dumbbells, with the most obvious being their space-saving design: No matter which adjustable dumbbells you choose, you can guarantee they'll take up less space than the sets of traditional dumbbells they replace.

Another attractive benefit of adjustable dumbbells is that they're more cost-effective than multiple sets of traditional dumbbells. A lot of the options on this list aren't exactly budget buys, we know. But building out a weight rack with 5-15 sets of high-quality traditional dumbbells can add up in cost even quicker.

This comes down to three things: space, personal preference, and how you plan to use your dumbbells. If you have unlimited space, you can definitely consider standard dumbbells.

"If you're building out a home gym and especially if you like to train accessory motions and work through a full range of motion, you still can't beat standard dumbbells," explains Samuel.

"They're going to be more durable, have better weight distribution for most moves, and, as cool as some adjustment dial might be, there's nothing more efficient than literally putting a 35-pound dumbbell down and picking a 40-pounder up."

But if you're in tight confines or like to work out on the go, opt for a good adjustable option. "You can load a pair of Powerblocks in your trunk much more easily than you can load 10 pairs of dumbbells for a road trip."

You'll also want to consider how often you'll drop your dumbbells. Even the best, most durable adjustable dumbbells on this list still have weight-switching mechanisms and won't hold up to being routinely dropped from a few feet in the air after a set of shoulder presses as well as standard dumbbells.

The weight of adjustable dumbbells depends on your fitness level and goals. Typically, they come in two main categories: those that max out at around 50 pounds per dumbbell and those that start at 50 pounds and get way heavier.

For beginners and folks looking to engage in moderate strength training at home, a set that maxes out at 50 pounds per dumbbell should suffice. They offer a range of weights for a wide variety of exercises and are a great starting point. Beginners can work on everything from biceps curls to overhead presses to squats with these.

Now, if you're a seasoned lifter, powerlifter, or someone aiming to build strength, opt for a pair of adjustable dumbbells that can go well above 50 pounds per bell. Adjustable sets from SMRTFT can offer a max of 80 pounds and 100 pounds per bell, respectively. For experienced lifters, added weight means greater versatility in tackling heavy exercises and challenging yourself.

Just like standard dumbbells, adjustable dumbbells are safe when used correctly and with proper form. But, as with any type of fitness equipment, there are some safety considerations to keep in mind.

It's important to choose adjustable dumbbells that are well-made and constructed from durable materials. If you're using an old-school model with removable plates, make sure they're securely attached to the handle before you start your lift.

The shape, feel, and weight distribution of adjustable dumbbells can take some getting used to, depending on the model you're working with. Because they may feel different compared to standard dumbbells in movements you do regularly, it's important to focus on slow, controlled movements and proper form throughout your workout (especially as you acclimate to them).

#4795. How Europe’s battery passport could have a big impact on US e-bikes

Europe is preparing to introduce a new requirement that could change how electric bicycle batteries are tracked, repaired, recycled, and potentially even resold. Starting in February 2027, new e-bike batteries sold in the European Union will be required to carry a digital battery passport, giving each battery its own digital identity and making important information about its origins and characteristics accessible throughout its lifetime.

And while the rules are European, their impact could eventually reach American e-bike riders, too.

The battery passport requirement comes from the EU’s 2023 Batteries Regulation, which established new standards for battery sustainability, traceability, and transparency. The rules cover several categories of batteries, including those used in electric cars, electric bicycles, electric scooters, and other light electric vehicles.

Beginning February 18, 2027, newly placed batteries in these categories will need digital passports accessible through QR codes. Scanning the code will provide access to information about the battery, though exactly what users can see will depend on their authorization level.

The information can include details such as the battery’s manufacturer, chemistry, capacity, cycle count, carbon footprint, and materials used in its construction. The system also provides for information about battery performance and durability, including data related to battery health and degradation.

That last part could be particularly interesting for electric bicycle owners.

Anyone who has purchased a used electric bicycle knows that the battery is often one of the biggest unknowns. A bike might look nearly new, but its battery could have hundreds of charge cycles under its belt and significantly reduced capacity.

Even a quick test ride before a secondhand e-bike purchase may fail to demonstrate just how little capacity remains in a heavily used battery.

With replacement e-bike batteries costing hundreds of dollars, that’s a pretty important detail.

The battery passport system could eventually help address that problem by making battery information more transparent. However, there’s an important distinction: the regulations don’t necessarily guarantee that everyday consumers will be able to scan a QR code and immediately see a battery’s remaining health percentage. Some of that information may be restricted to authorized users.

Even so, the system could help repair shops, recyclers, and secondhand buyers better understand the batteries they’re dealing with.

It could also make life more complicated for e-bike manufacturers, especially smaller brands that will now need to ensure their batteries meet the new documentation and traceability requirements.

There’s currently no equivalent nationwide battery passport requirement for electric bicycles in the United States, but that doesn’t mean American riders won’t eventually benefit.

I think it's really great that European consumer protection laws have a global impact because of the size of the European single market, and that they make life just a little bit easier for consumers all over the world. USB-C was just the beginning—there's more to come!

Many major e-bike manufacturers sell their products in both Europe and North America. US-based companies like Trek and Specialized have major markets in Europe, and will have to comply with the new law. Chinese companies and other Asian manufacturers will also need to produce compliant batteries. Once those companies have developed systems to track individual batteries and provide digital passports for their European products, they may find it easier to extend those systems to their American models rather than maintain entirely separate processes.

That doesn’t mean US-bound batteries will automatically receive passports, but it could create an interesting spillover effect.

And considering how expensive e-bike batteries can be, anything that makes it easier to understand their condition, verify their origins, or facilitate repairs could be a welcome development.

For now, Europe is leading the charge on battery transparency. But if the system proves useful, American e-bike riders might eventually get some of the same benefits without waiting for Washington to catch up.

#4794. 3 Anxiety Resets From an OCD Therapist With OCD

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated November 12, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

“Sorry, my hand is shaking,” my client says.

We are in the middle of an exposure exercise for his obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD). He experiences terrifying intrusive thoughts about harming his loved ones, and my job is to help him confront those fears without resorting to compulsions. My client is holding a knife to the small of my back.

“I know it's hard, but stay with the exposure for another minute,” I reply.

As I sit with my client and allow the anxiety of the moment to wash over him, I ask my client to rate his distress on a scale of 1 to 10.

I am an OCD therapist, and I practice an objectively strange type of therapy. I help my clients engage in exposures—brave acts that fly in the face of their fears—while resisting their compulsions.

I love being an OCD therapist. Exposure and response prevention (ERP) is vastly preferable to trying to talk my clients out of their fears. Reassurance rarely works for long. The only thing that can convince my client that he won’t hurt me is being in a position where he could.

My clients are kindhearted, earnest humans who suffer from the same disorder that made me feel alone and scared for most of my 20s. The fear of harming someone does not equate to the intent to harm someone. I myself grappled mightily with this confusing thought pattern and learned to trust myself again.

But there are moments when my professionalism and empathy come up against a formidable foe: my own nervous system.

Sometimes, my nervous system forgets that I am safe. Sometimes my nervous system doesn’t understand time and place and, most importantly for the knife exposure, context. Despite all the work I've done, I still experience fear, anxiety, doubt, and the occasional panic attack.

And my experience is not unique. Many therapists are wounded healers. We love this work because we have lived this work.

One thing I've learned about mental health recovery is that we are never done. The goal isn't to eliminate anxiety forever. It's to develop the tools to move through it without allowing it to control our lives.

When I cannot stay present and grounded for my own therapy session, I count on three resourcing techniques that I learned from eye movement desensitization and reprocessing (EMDR), a therapy technique that I underwent as a patient. When my body forgets my professional training, I use techniques from EMDR to guide myself back to the present moment.

Butterfly tapping is a technique that involves gently alternating taps on either side of the body. It's a subtle movement you can try almost anywhere, including at a crowded party or during a stressful conversation. (Or, in my case, in a knife exposure with my client)

Cross your arms against your chest and place each hand on the opposite collarbone. Now, gently and rhythmically begin alternating taps from one side to the other.

Continue for a short period, noticing the rhythm and how your body responds.

The alternating stimulation and repetitive movement may help you feel more grounded. There is no need to force yourself to feel calm or continue if the exercise feels uncomfortable.

Sometimes, a moment of physical connection is all you need to find your footing again.

Your mind can be remarkably unkind, especially when you feel anxious. Trauma can encode negative thought patterns into your brain, telling you things like “I cannot handle feeling uncomfortable” or “I am not strong enough.”

Before heading into a stressful situation, you can choose a phrase that reminds you of how you want to respond when discomfort arises.

Repeat your phrase gently when you need a reminder.

I like to take a photo of my mantra and set it as my phone's home screen because I tend to pick up my phone and glance at it when I'm uncomfortable.

An important distinction for anyone with OCD: A mantra should offer encouragement, not become a ritual you must repeat until your fear disappears. The aim is to develop tolerance for uncomfortable feelings, not compulsively reassure ourselves that nothing bad will happen.

EMDR can open up strong emotions, but it also guides people on how to temporarily put them away.

For this exercise, you may close your eyes, if appropriate in the situation, and imagine a container that can hold the feelings or concerns you aren't ready to address.

It can be a chest, lockbox, jar, drawer, or anything you can vividly picture.

Now imagine placing a troubling experience inside that container. You can return to the experience later, when you have the time and resources for processing.

I use this for a nervous system spike during my therapy workday. My job is to stay present for my client, so I put any reactions in a container and set them aside temporarily.

The goal isn't to suppress feelings or avoid necessary emotional work. If you have OCD, be mindful that this exercise doesn't become another way to neutralize intrusive thoughts or escape uncertainty.

Instead, think of it as giving yourself permission to choose when and how to address an experience that deserves your attention.

As an OCD therapist, I have learned that recovery doesn't mean becoming a person who never experiences anxiety.

In fact, the entire premise of ERP is that we can learn to face discomfort without relying on compulsions to make it disappear.

The three techniques can offer support when anxiety feels overwhelming, but they aren't substitutes for treatment. No anxiety reset should become a ritual that you perform perfectly.

By the end of our session, my client's hand is no longer shaking. He tells me his distress has fallen to a “2 out of 10.”

“Good job staying with the discomfort,” I say, mostly to him, but also a bit to myself.

Here we are, two imperfect nervous systems, finding our way back to the present moment and moving forward with recovery.

Shapiro, F. (2001). Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing: Basic Principles, Protocols, and Procedures (2nd ed.). Guilford Press.

#4793. After 471,625 miles, this Chevy Bolt is doing better than you think [video]

Wondering how long your new electric car might last? This 2019 Chevrolet Bolt EV is proving that electric vehicles can rack up miles with the best of them – and its owner is committed to taking it past the half million mile mark.

You’d think a 250,000 mile Ford Mustang Mach-E maintaining 92% of its battery life, a 360,000 mile Hyundai IONIQ 5 with 87% battery health still intact, and a half-dozen stories of Tesla Model S, 3, and Y ride share vehicles racking up six figures on their odometers later would do more to convince the slow adopters and doubting Thomases of the world that EV batteries are built to last. The good news is that the evidence keeps piling up, and this latest example of electric endurance is a good one.

On the Out of Spec Renew YouTube channel, the crew took in a 2019 Chevy Bolt EV – one of the most affordable new EVs you could buy in 2019 – that had more than 470,000 miles on the clock and 330,000 miles on its post-recall battery. That’s nearly half a million miles on the original electric motor, and it’s still got more to go.

Average gas car lasts ~150k miles. For sure requiring more maintenance to reach that mileage than an EV. Achieving ~500k on the original motor and over 300k on a battery is quite impressive.

Getting towards the 100k mile mark in both our EVs. Both feel like brand new and have required almost no maintenance - a fraction of what would be required with ICE. Look forward to hitting 200k and beyond in each. For the first time in over 30 years of driving, I don’t look forward to replacing our cars as they get over 100k miles - rather I look forward to the next 100k miles of driving.

Out of Spec Renew replaced the 2019’s battery pack that was experiencing serious battery faults and cell-voltage imbalances with a stable, lower-mile example from a 2017 model. Once it was up and in, they got the car powered up, programmed, and driving again, putting the owner on track to reach the 500,000 mile milestone (sorry) in their trusty steed.

The OOSR crew paid $1,800 for the “new” battery, but estimates consumers would pay between $2,500-3,000 for the a similar pack. You can check out the full battery replacement video, below, then let us know how far you plan on taking your EV in the comments.

#4792. I Am Turning 40, and Refusing to Apologize for It

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 12, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

Yes, I celebrate the month. (Don’t @ me!) It was actually something I started doing in college. My birthday (the actual day) falls close to Thanksgiving, so many of my friends would be leaving campus right around the time I was getting ready to celebrate. I also had a roommate whose birthday was close to Christmas, so we started celebrating early.

The trend caught on (whether it caught on or I pushed it, I will never know). This worked well until my 21st birthday, which, as we all know, cannot legally be celebrated early—at least not if you want your special bar drink in hand.

If you’re rolling your eyes and thinking I appear a bit arrogant, bear with me for a moment while I explain. While celebrating and having fun with friends was, of course, fun, these celebrations actually served a deeper purpose for me—although I didn't know it at the time. When college ended, I found myself alone again, thrown back into a world where my only source of support—my family—was unsafe and unstable. Home was scary.

Celebrating myself became a way of honoring my own journey. It was a way of recognizing the strength it took to navigate the year, and the safety I was learning to create within myself. It became a "Yay, Kaytee, you made it another year. You did it." Years later, I still have that same message, but it has become something deeper.

This was almost 20 years ago. This month I turn 40. An age where we, especially women, are told to stop celebrating. An age we are taught to dread. All month, I’ve received messages like these from others, including my own family:

“I bet you’re not excited about this birthday.”

"I was going to send you a card, but I imagine you don't want the reminder."

“I bet you won’t celebrate the whole month anymore.”

And I can’t help but wonder: Why? Why are we so negative about aging? We mourn when people die young, yet somehow shame those of us who are fortunate enough to keep living. We grieve the years someone never got to experience, while simultaneously treating the years we do get as something to fear.

I refuse to participate in this ageism. I have always celebrated my birthday, and I always will. Not just in the traditional, celebratory sense (I mean, cake is always nice), but as a way of honoring myself and all that I have become. I am always stumped at how much it bothers people that I dare embrace myself as an aging woman.

I am proud of who I am today. I love myself more today than I ever did when I was young. I no longer self-medicate or mistreat my body in the ways I had to to survive my childhood. I am happier and healthier now than I ever have been before. I have come so far and learned so much since that 20-year-old college student who celebrated her birthday with her roommates for a week straight, in one of the few places where she felt safe (but was unable to verbalize this at the time). I wish I could go back and tell her that someday it won't be so scary, and she won't have to put on a fake persona of strength to continue the denial. I would tell her not only that she would survive, but how much she would survive, and how much of a life she would eventually build for herself. I think she would be pretty damn proud, too. (And maybe a bit relieved to see a light at the end of what felt like a long, dark tunnel.)

Happy birthday month to me. And to all of us who have survived and are surviving. I hope you find a way to honor and celebrate yourself, too.

#4791. Bestselling US e-bike Lectric XP4 relaunched in limited-edition with new colors and gear

The Lectric XP series has become something of an institution in the American electric bicycle market. As the country’s best-selling e-bike lineup, it’s helped put hundreds of thousands of riders on two wheels, largely thanks to its combination of affordable pricing, impressive performance, and practical features. It’s become the go-to electric bike in the US, but that hasn’t made Lectric complacent. Instead, the company is continuing to innovate.

Now, Lectric is giving its flagship XP4 a fresh makeover with three new limited-edition versions, each sporting a unique color and a new collection of accessories and upgrades designed for different types of riders, from urban assault roles to conquering your favorite off-road fishing spots.

The new Lectric XP4 Limited Editions come in three flavors: District, (black) Jubilee (pink), and Ridge (green). Each is priced at $1,399 and includes a 750W motor, upgraded accessories, and a distinctive matte paint job. That’s just a $100 premium over the existing XP 750, yet comes with a whole new host of accessories designed specifically for each special edition model.

So while the underlying bike remains largely unchanged from the bones of the XP 750, the new packages are designed to make the XP4 even more useful straight out of the box.

The District edition is aimed squarely at urban commuters, sporting a stealthy Matte Black finish and an accessory package designed for daily transportation.

That includes two waterproof pannier bags, a redesigned LevelUp rear cargo rack, a heavy-duty bike lock, and an upgraded high-output headlight. There’s also a fast charger, suspension seat post with comfort saddle, and handlebar phone mount.

It’s essentially a ready-made commuter setup, particularly for riders looking to replace some of their car trips with an e-bike.

The Jubilee edition takes a more casual approach, arriving in a distinctive Matte Thistle colorway. Designed for neighborhood cruising, weekend errands, and trips to the local farmers market, it swaps the commuter-focused panniers for a front and rear cargo package and a small roll-top bag.

It also includes the upgraded headlight, lock, fast charger, suspension seat post, comfort saddle, and phone mount.

Finally, the Ridge edition is built for riders who prefer their adventures a bit farther from the pavement.

Finished in Matte Forest green, the Ridge comes with front and rear cargo accessories for carrying outdoor gear, plus a fishing rod holder on the High-Step version. The Step-Thru model instead receives a weather-resistant roll-top bag.

Like the other two editions, the Ridge also includes the upgraded lighting, lock, charger, and comfort accessories.

“We wanted to deliver ready-made, purpose-built setups that empower our community to jump on and ride without having to configure their gear from scratch,” explained Lectric co-founder and CEO Levi Conlow.

Conlow also seems particularly proud of the new finishes, calling them the three best paint jobs Lectric has produced in its seven-year history.

While the new colors and accessory bundles are the main attraction, the bikes retain the same core features that helped make the XP4 such a popular choice.

That includes Lectric’s in-house developed dynamic torque sensor, which measures how hard the rider pedals to deliver a more natural-feeling electric assist experience.

The bikes also feature hydraulic disc brakes, an 8-speed Shimano Altus drivetrain, and a full-color TFT display.

As with the standard XP4, riders get the familiar folding frame design, integrated turn signals and brake lights, and 20-inch puncture-resistant mixed-terrain tires.

All three limited editions are available in both High-Step and Step-Thru frame configurations.

At $1,399, the new models aren’t trying to reinvent the XP4 formula. Instead, they’re offering a more fully equipped version of a bike that has already proven itself with American riders.

And that’s probably a smart move. Lectric has built its reputation on delivering an impressive amount of e-bike for the money, and bundling useful accessories into a relatively affordable package plays right into that strategy.

The limited-edition models are available now, though Lectric says quantities are strictly limited.

For riders who have been considering an XP4 but wanted something a bit more distinctive than the standard colors, these new editions could be a compelling reason to finally pull the trigger.

And for those looking to score an even better deal, Lectric has also officially kicked off its Black Friday sale.

The company is calling it its biggest sale of the year, with some of its lowest prices ever and discounts of up to $800 across its lineup.

So whether you’re eyeing one of the new limited-edition XP4 models or another e-bike in Lectric’s extensive catalog, now could be a particularly good time to buy.

#4790. The Universality of Privilege and Inheritance of Excellence

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 12, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

The word privilege has somehow evolved linguistically to be viewed negatively. It has also come to imply an unearned advantage or an unfair benefit held by one group at another's expense.

Throughout human history, privilege has meant something quite different: privilege has emerged when individuals and/or groups apply merit, achievement, competence, and excellence in ways that expand possibilities for everyone. I refer to this as the MACE Principle.

Research shows that high levels of expertize and exceptional performance emerge through sustained practice, learning, and skill refinement rather than arising spontaneously. In this sense, such accomplishments and the benefits they create for subsequent generations are among the oldest features of human civilization (Ericsson, 2008; Srivastava & Das, 2015).

Nearly three million years ago, our distant ancestors fashioned the first stone tools. The first person to shape stone into a cutting implement created something far more significant than a simple object. That innovation gave the entire group a practical advantage.

The collective also gained a privilege. The tribe could now cut hunted and gathered food and, self-evidently, share their food far more efficiently and much more quickly. Survival itself became easier.

Consequently, the privilege created by that stone-tool innovation was not confined to the inventor; it became a significant benefit and privilege enjoyed by the collective (Kivell, 2015; Stout, 2011).

The same pattern recurs throughout history. The invention of the wheel transformed transport and trade. Once developed, the wheel's benefits and the privilege it created extended far beyond its creator.

Entire communities far removed from the original invention gained the privilege of moving goods and people more efficiently. What began as an achievement of human ingenuity became a shared privilege and an immense social advantage beyond its original location (Kivell, 2015; Stout, 2011).

Perhaps no invention demonstrates this process more dramatically than the printing press. Developed in the 15th century by Johannes Gutenberg in Mainz, within the Holy Roman Empire (present-day Germany), the printing press fundamentally altered humanity's relationship with the development and advancement of knowledge.

Reading, writing, collective information, ideas, and knowledge, once largely confined to a comparatively small number of individuals, could now be reproduced, preserved, and distributed on a scale that was never before possible.

Reading and writing ceased to be “a mystery” for a select number of individuals or a “select” group. As with the stone tool and the wheel before it, the printing press created new benefits and privileges, consequently moving these benefits and privileges from the few to the many.

Although history informs us (as with all inventions and achievements), the resulting benefits and privileges were not always distributed equally.

However, even with this being the case, with the wider dissemination of knowledge (following the invention of the 15th-century printing press), the benefits of this invention extended far beyond Gutenberg and transformed what future generations could achieve (Jara-Figueroa et al., 2019; Triggle & Triggle, 2017).

Consider what followed. For approximately three million years, humanity crafted tools, built settlements, established civilizations, constructed cities, developed metallurgy, crossed oceans, fought wars, and created empires.

During this period, countless innovations delivered immense benefits and privilege. Yet the accumulation and transmission of knowledge remained comparatively limited.

Then, within about five centuries of the invention of the printing press, humanity witnessed an unprecedented acceleration in the growth and development of knowledge (Jara-Figueroa et al., 2019; Triggle & Triggle, 2017).

In the 18th century, Edward Jenner laid the foundations of modern immunization with the first successful smallpox vaccination (Riedel, 2005).

In the 20th century, the United States sent three men to the Moon: Neil Armstrong, the first human to walk on its surface; Buzz Aldrin, the second; and Michael Collins, who remained in lunar orbit as part of the mission.

These achievements produced further benefits and privilege, as earlier innovations had. They reflected humanity's expanding capacity to preserve, transmit, and build upon knowledge. The printing press transformed reading, writing, ideas, and information into a far more widely shared social benefit and privilege for the many (Triggle & Triggle, 2017).

In doing so, it expanded the benefits and privilege available to successive generations and helped create the conditions for scientific, technological, and civilizational advancement to proceed at a pace previously unknown in human history (Jara-Figueroa et al., 2019; Triggle & Triggle, 2017).

The same principle applied across medicine, engineering, agriculture, chemistry, and countless other fields.

Vaccines, clean water systems, supermarkets, automobiles, telecommunications, digital technologies, and now artificial intelligence all exist because individuals pursued excellence in their respective domains.

The benefits of those achievements are enjoyed not merely by their creators but by millions, and even potentially billions, of people (Tewksbury et al., 1980; Yu & Liu, 2021).

Throughout history, parents have generally sought to provide advantages, opportunities, benefits, and privilege to their children, just as previous generations sought to provide them to those who followed.

Civilization itself can therefore be understood as the cumulative result of countless individuals attempting to improve the circumstances inherited by the next generation (Gulyas & Powell, 2019; Stout & Hecht, 2017).

This does not self-evidently mean that every benefit or privilege is distributed equally; it never has and it never will.

It does mean, however, that inventions and achievements, no matter what they were, enriched lives, from the smallest tribes to the largest civilizations, because there were individuals who invented something that changed what previously existed, and with this, benefits and privilege arose (Dean et al., 2014; Tewksbury et al., 1980).

The story of human civilization is the story of expanding everyone's potential for privilege, but not a guarantee. Through innovation, discovery, and excellence, however, humanity has repeatedly turned extraordinary achievements into benefits that potentially eventually become available to the broader populace.

The greatest privilege is that each generation inherits the achievements of those who came before and can contribute new ones for those yet to come (Dean et al., 2014; Stout & Hecht, 2017).

#4789. Electric trucks hit 50% of China’s heavy truck sales, diesel demand falls

Electric trucks made up 50.3% of all heavy trucks sold in China in September. That’s 33,100 electric big rigs in a single month, up 37% from a year ago, while the overall heavy-truck market shrank by 21%.

And it’s showing up in the oil data. China’s diesel demand is on track to fall by about 230,000 barrels per day this year, and trucks running on batteries and natural gas are doing most of the work.

In 2024, new-energy vehicles accounted for 13.6% of heavy trucks (12 tonnes and up) sold in China. In 2025, sales nearly tripled to 231,100 units, up 182%, for a 28.9% share.

December 2025 hit 53.9%, but that was a rush. Buyers piled in before trade-in subsidies expired and new purchase tax costs kicked in, and the share dropped back to about 23% by March.

Then it came right back. Through the first nine months of 2026, China sold 226,400 electric heavy trucks, up 64%, for a 38.1% share. That’s already almost as many as in all of 2025, with a quarter still to go. In tractors, the big rigs that pull long-haul trailers, the September share hit 64.5%.

That’s well ahead of Beijing’s own plan. This year, 11 government bodies set a target of 40% new-energy heavy-truck sales by 2030, along with 1.6 million of them on the road, 30,000 km of zero-carbon freight corridors and about 3,000 charging and swap stations. The market blew past that sales target four years early on a monthly basis, and CATL now says new-energy trucks will be half of China’s annual truck sales by 2028.

It comes down to cost. In most uses, an electric heavy truck in China is now cheaper to own and run than a diesel one, and fleets run that math every day.

CATL claims savings of about 0.6 yuan per km. Independent numbers are more measured, but still favorable: a study by the ICCT and China’s CATARC found battery-electric trucks about 19% cheaper per tonne-km than diesel in good conditions, though they lose that edge at low annual mileage or when battery weight eats into payload.

Charging time is the other objection, and China’s answer is swapping. CATL’s Qiji brand operated about 300 heavy-truck swap stations at the end of 2025 and plans 900 by the end of this year and 2,000 in 2027. In August, it agreed to pay 2.56 billion yuan (about $370 million) for nearly 25% of Qiyuan Green Power, China’s largest heavy-truck swap operator with more than 1,600 charging and swap stations. Its new standardized packs hold 432 kWh and 513 kWh and swap in about five minutes.

CATL is already taking the swapping model to Europe with Octopus Energy.

The trucks themselves are domestic. XCMG led the segment in 2025 with a 15.4% share, ahead of SANY and FAW Jiefang, and the top three held 42.9% of the market. CATL supplied 60% of the batteries.

For years, the alternative to diesel trucks in China was liquefied natural gas. LNG trucks took nearly 30% of the market in 2024, when gas was much cheaper than diesel.

Now they’re losing to batteries. According to Kpler, LNG trucks had a 37% share of heavy-duty registrations in March, against 23% for electric. By July, electric was at 47% and LNG had collapsed to 11%. Monthly LNG truck registrations fell from more than 30,000 to about 6,200.

So China is skipping the “bridge fuel” phase for trucks almost as fast as it started it.

China’s diesel consumption already peaked. Rhodium Group found that diesel refinery runs topped out in April 2023, and apparent consumption dropped from 4.7 million barrels per day then to 4.0 million barrels per day in April 2025.

2026 is the steepest drop yet. Kpler estimates diesel demand fell about 420,000 barrels per day year-over-year in May, roughly 10%, and 460,000 in June. It expects a decline of about 230,000 barrels per day for the full year and only a 64,000 barrel-per-day rebound in 2027.

Kpler puts the gross diesel displacement from alternative trucks at about 680,000 barrels per day this year: roughly 450,000 from the LNG fleet built in recent years and 230,000 from electric trucks. Road freight still grew about 3% through July. China is moving more goods with less diesel.

There’s a catch. The fuel price spike this spring, tied to the Iran war, cut demand on its own and pushed more fleets toward electric. But that only explains part of it, and the fleet is still early: electric trucks will be only about 8% of China’s heavy trucks on the road by the end of 2026, according to Kpler. Every year of 40-50% sales shares compounds the diesel losses.

Europe is growing fast from a tiny base. ACEA data shows 5,120 heavy electric trucks (16 tonnes and up) registered in the EU through September, up 59.9%, for a 2.5% share. That’s up from 1.7% a year ago, but diesel still took 91.7% of all EU truck registrations.

A few countries stand out. Switzerland is at 24%, Norway 14.4%, the Netherlands 11.1% and Sweden 10.3%. Germany registered the most units at 1,722, but that’s only a 4.2% share.

The US doesn’t publish an official electric Class 8 sales figure, and that tells you something. The best indicator is the recent order for 2,500 Tesla Semis through ZET SCALE, which would roughly double the number of electric Class 8 trucks on US roads. Against about 230,000 Class 8 trucks sold per year, the electric share is well under 1%.

Price is the big difference. The ICCT puts the median electric Class 8 tractor in the US at $411,200, against $172,500 for diesel. Federal tax credits for commercial EVs ended in 2025, and California shelved the rule that would have required fleets to buy zero-emission trucks.

This is the biggest under-covered story in the EV industry right now.

Everyone argued for years about whether electric semis could work. Range, weight, charging, cost. China settled it the boring way. It got the price of a battery-electric heavy truck close enough to diesel, built swap stations along freight routes, and let fleet operators do what fleet operators always do: pick the cheapest truck per kilometer.

And the result is showing up where it matters, in oil demand. Trucks are where diesel lives. Displacing a quarter of a million barrels a day in one year, with electric trucks still only around 8% of the fleet, means we’re still early on this curve.

The contrast with the US is hard to watch. America has Tesla, a Semi factory in Nevada built for 50,000 trucks a year, and some of the best freight corridors in the world for electrification. But electric Class 8 trucks cost 2.4 times as much as diesel here, the federal incentives are gone, and the market is under 1%. The ZET SCALE order is real progress. But it came from shippers pooling their demand, and twe have yet to see these trucks get delivered.

China having a lot of phev and EV vehicles has helped with oil pricing around the world, more notably in the current american-caused oil crisis. It would be worse if they were all traditional powered cars and trucks.

Now to be clear, I'm not saying that it has made a massive impact or is even the only reason why the oil crisis isn't much worse, it's just one of a few steps China made to reduce the impact of the oil crisis. But going electric everywhere we can has a stabilizing effect when oil shocks show up

Europe at least has the regulation, and its best markets, at 10% to 24%, are roughly where China was in 2024 and 2025.

The question now is how long Chinese truck makers stay home. SANY and BYD already sell electric trucks in Europe, and CATL is building the swap network for them. If those trucks can come close to China’s pricing, how long can Western truck makers keep charging 2x diesel?

Diesel trucks aren’t the only thing batteries are displacing. At home, pairing solar with an EV or a home battery can cut your energy bills dramatically. With electricity rates up almost 10% last year and expected to keep climbing, going solar is one of the best ways to protect yourself against rising costs. #4788. What Perpetuates the Family Cycle of Violence?

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 12, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

This post is the second in an occasional series on the family cycle of violence.

In May 2026, we posted "Do Abused Parents Become Child Abusers?" which we subtitled: "Multiple interacting factors shape the intergenerational cycle of maltreatment." That post is intended to be the foundation for an undetermined number of future posts examining the intergenerational transmission of increased risk for maltreatment to the offspring of parents who were maltreated themselves as children. The larger focus of this series is the two-part question: “Can we break the family cycle of violence?” and “If so, how?”

The key points of the earlier post are that the single most powerful risk factor for a child being maltreated is having a parent who was maltreated. Most (~70 percent) parents with child maltreatment histories do not become abusive parents. However, the risk of becoming an abusive parent is 6 to 12 times higher than for parents without a childhood maltreatment history. The mechanisms underlying this increased risk may be indirect (e.g., decreased parental vigilance) or direct (perpetration). This increased risk is a result of multiple, interacting levels of factors (e.g., depression, dissociation, substance abuse, domestic violence, unsafe households, poverty, neighborhood factors, public policies). To be cost-effective, prevention programs must seek to address the most critical shared underlying factors synergistically.

The post also notes that individuals can promote positive social change by openly acknowledging their own and others’ childhood maltreatment, thereby validating survivors, reducing stigma, and keeping public attention focused on this enormous public health problem.

How do we tease out the most critical factors on which to focus the always limited prevention resources? This conundrum is further complicated by the need to follow these multiple interacting factors in large general population samples for decades. Not to mention that even the most dedicated family violence researchers are lifetime-limited to studying only two or three generations during their careers.

There is another way, however, to get at least a ballpark understanding of the interacting factors that promote the family cycle of violence across generations. This involves the use of Agent-Based Models. ABMs are computer simulations in which individual “people” are represented by computational entities (agents) that can behave and interact with each other according to predefined rules (Smaldino, 2023). Think SimCity or other computer games that involve characters with past histories, have current and future agendas, and develop complicated interrelationships that can evolve apart and together “over time” to produce a range of outcomes.

Computer simulations, both equation-based and agent-based, are widely used to investigate systems and processes that are too large, too complex, and too costly to study on real-world scales. Examples include the weather, epidemics, and the Big Bang. One advantage is that computer simulations can be run thousands of times as needed to sweep through the numerous combinations of potential variables, searching for fundamental trajectories, collapses, singularities, best fits with real-world data, and critical tipping points that may serve as prevention targets.

Perhaps the best way to understand an ABM is to briefly describe a model simulating the intergenerational transmission of risk for maltreatment of offspring. The model begins with a number of unmarried adult males and females (typically 50 each to limit CPU time, as this breeds hundreds of new agents over three to five generations). These male and female adults are randomly scattered on a multicolored checkerboard “city” map of neighborhoods that hold different levels of risk for children born in them.

In generation 0, each agent (males are blue, females green) is randomly assigned a lifespan and a level of positive and negative “childhood” baggage, some of which may be passed to offspring. These adults proceed to seek out an opposite-gender partner with which to have “children.” Each adult can “see” the childhood baggage of the adults immediately around them and chooses a partner based on a variable called “match” (more on “match” below).

If there is not a suitable “match” in sight, agents take off randomly seeking one. Some agents never meet their “match” and never have children. In addition, each agent is randomly assigned a lifespan at birth. When their lifespan is up, they die and are removed from the board.

When a pair of agents do match—that is, their combined childhood baggage is within the bounds set by the “match” variable—they can “marry,” and every so often they breed a child. They also move around as a family, landing in positive or negative neighborhoods, which affect their growing children. The children pass through three developmental stages (infancy, childhood, adolescence), eventually becoming adults who carry forward into the next generation the risk accumulated over their childhoods. Childhood risk may be concentrated at certain developmental stages or distributed randomly across development, with the weight that earlier acquired risk has a greater lifetime impact.

When the adolescents become young adults, they leave their families to seek a partner with which to have their own children. A new “generation” occurs when a specified percentage (typically 70 percent) of children born to the preceding generation have reached adulthood. Models are typically run for three to five generations, and a combination of inputs is examined for their effects on outputs such as percent of population abused, average risk scores, female-to-male victim ratios, or geographic density of abuse/non-abuse clusters.

A typical experiment involves sweeping through a pre-set combination of variables (e.g., threshold for domestic violence, gender sensitivity coefficients, degree of match) to see how various combinations affect selected outputs. Typically, each combination of inputs is run at least 100 times, and the results are saved to a file for detailed statistical analyses.

The “match” variable was included among the input parameters because of research on the nonrandom or “assortative” mating of individuals with mental health diagnoses. Epidemiologists have found that individuals with mental health diagnoses are significantly more likely to partner with mates who have the same or related diagnoses than are comparison subjects with medical diagnoses having similar degrees of lifestyle impact, such as diabetes or epilepsy. Large-scale Swedish studies have found the frequency of assortative mating for 11 major mental health conditions ranges between two and six times that of equivalent medical conditions (Nordsletten et al., 2016).

“All computer models are wrong, but some are useful” —Old programmer saying

Somewhat to my surprise, “match” has turned out to be a critical variable driving rates of intergenerational transmission of risk for maltreatment of offspring. The ABM finds that the impact of two parents with childhood maltreatment histories significantly increases the risk that their offspring will also suffer maltreatment. Much of this effect is driven by the increased rate of domestic violence found when both parents have a childhood maltreatment history.

Thus, among the potential insights gained from the ABM model is that a childhood history of maltreatment in both parents is potentially a major risk factor for continuation of the family cycle of violence. How often this double parental maltreatment history occurs in real life is difficult to establish at present. However, if we accept that the assortative mating research on psychiatric diagnoses also applies to some degree to individuals with trauma-associated psychiatric disorders, it could happen among a significant number of family violence cases.

Computer models are “thinking machines.” They require their authors to think through dynamic processes and to formulate and parameterize the resulting algorithms. An ABM model is not real life, but sometimes it can yield insights that would be impossible to glean from real life without investing many years and millions of dollars.

Smaldino, P.E. (2023). Modeling Social Behavior: Mathematical and Agent-Based Models of Social Dynamics and Cultural Evolution. Princeton University Press.

Nordsletten, A.E. et al. (2016) Patterns of Nonrandom Mating Within and Across 11 Major Psychiatric Disorders. JAMA Psychiatry. 2016;73(4):354–361.
