#4767. Dog-ma: Jung, Synchronicity, and the Beach Yoga Class That Was Ruff

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 12, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

I sat cross-legged in the sand, doing my best impression of someone with their thoughts under control, when the yoga instructor said the line every meditator has heard a thousand times: Your mind is like a puppy. It wanders off; you gently bring it back. It wanders off again; you bring it back again. No yelling. No drama. Just patient redirection, over and over, forever, amen.

And at that exact moment—not as a vague afterthought, but right then—a woman 20 feet away in front of the class, behind the instructor, and in front of the ocean, was locked in a full-contact wrestling match with an actual dog on an actual leash. Pulling. Tugging. The dog wanted the water, she wanted the boardwalk, and neither of them was interested in gentle redirection. It was the least zen scene on the entire beach, unfolding in real time as a soundtrack to a lecture about zen.

I opened one eye. I am fairly sure I laughed out loud, which is not great yoga etiquette.

Here's the thing about moments like that: You can shrug them off as a coincidence or let them stop you in your tracks. I let this one stop me, because it did something a metaphor alone never quite manages—it made the metaphor physical. I didn't just hear that my mind is like a puppy. I watched a mind-sized puppy misbehave in real time, a very short distance from where I sat trying to master mine.

Carl Jung had a word for this—synchronicity—meaningful coincidences that seem to carry significance beyond ordinary cause and effect. Jung wasn't claiming the universe is a puppeteer pulling strings so your yoga class gets better sound effects. He was pointing at something subtler: that meaning sometimes arrives sideways, through timing, rather than head-on, through explanation.

For decades, that idea lived mostly in Jungian circles, treated as a little too mystical for serious psychology to touch. But it turns out some very serious psychologists have been touching it anyway. Pninit Russo-Netzer and Tamar Icekson, researchers who study meaning and well-being, spent years interviewing people about their synchronicity experiences—the goosebump moments, the "You would not believe what just happened" moments—and out of those interviews they built something researchers love and mystics tend to distrust: a model.

They call it REM, and no, it has nothing to do with sleep. It stands for: Receptiveness—being open, attentive, quietly available to what's happening around you (which, not coincidentally, is exactly what a beach at sunrise with your eyes half-closed is designed to produce). Then an Exceptional encounter—the unexpected event that rhymes with something already stirring inside you. And finally, Meaning-detecting—the moment you consciously connect the two and let it mean something.

Notice that meaning-detecting is a verb, not a lightning bolt. The dog and the puppy metaphor didn't hand me a revelation. I had to reach out and pick it up. Russo-Netzer and Icekson later built a whole scale around this—the Synchronicity Awareness and Meaning-Detecting Scale—and their data suggests something wonderfully unmystical: People who notice these moments and let them land tend to report more optimism, a stronger sense that life holds together, and higher life satisfaction. Not because coincidences are magic, but because noticing them is a skill, and it's a skill that keeps paying you back.

Which brings me to the dog, one more time. The woman eventually won. Or the dog decided the fight wasn't worth it; it's hard to say who negotiated whom. But watching it, I thought: That's what my brain does to me on a slow Wednesday when a worry won't drop the leash. And what the instructor was really teaching wasn't a metaphor about puppies at all. It was a rehearsal for exactly that moment on the beach—so that when my own mind starts pulling toward the water, I remember I'm allowed to just...turn, and walk, and not make it a fight.

I don't think the universe scheduled that dog for my benefit. I think the universe is simply generous with material, all the time, and most of it goes right past us because we're not receptive enough to catch it. That morning, for once, I paid just enough attention to catch the pitch. The dog never did learn to heel. Neither, most mornings, have I. But I’m a tad more hopeful.

Russo-Netzer, P., & Icekson, T. (2022). Engaging with life: Synchronicity experiences as a pathway to meaning and personal growth. Current Psychology, 41(2), 597–610. doi.org/10.1007/s12144-019-00595-1

Russo-Netzer, P., & Icekson, T. (2023). An underexplored pathway to life satisfaction: The development and validation of the synchronicity awareness and meaning-detecting scale. Frontiers in Psychology, 13, 1053296. doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2022.1053296

#4766. Obesity in Your 20s and 30s May Increase Cancer Risk Later in Life

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Younger adults with obesity may be more likely to develop cancer before midlife than those who maintain a moderate weight, according to a study published on October 26 in the Annals of Internal Medicine.

The risk for cancer became higher as weight increased. The highest rates were seen in those with severe obesity and abdominal obesity.

This highlights the potential importance of weight management in the prevention of early onset cancer.

Rates of both obesity and early onset cancer are rising among younger adults globally.

This study analyzed data from the Korean National Health Insurance Service database. The researchers identified 6,313,338 adults ages 20 to 39 who had no history of cancer and who underwent standardized national health screenings.

The researchers followed the participants for an average of 11 years.

Body mass index (BMI) was categorized into five groups ranging from underweight to class II obesity using the World Health Organization (WHO) criteria for Asian populations. Waist circumference was also measured as an indicator of abdominal adiposity.

During the analysis, the researchers adjusted for various factors such as:

Over the follow-up period, there were 151,893 cases of cancer among the participants. The incidence rate increased progressively based on obesity categories, from 1.84% in “normal-weight” individuals to 2.24% in class I obesity and 2.62% in class II obesity.

The strongest associations were seen in the following cancers:

Obesity was not associated with breast cancer diagnosed before the age of 50.

Ketan Thanki, MD, board certified colorectal surgeon with the MemorialCare Todd Cancer Institute at Long Beach Medical Center in Long Beach, CA, who wasn’t involved in the study, explained to Healthline that obesity itself causes states that promote cancer formation.

This current study focused on the Korean population. However, the connection between obesity and cancer risk is a global issue.

Previous research has shown that around 10% of all new cancer diagnoses in the United States are associated with obesity. Obesity also accounts for up to 50% of certain cancers, including endometrial and liver cancer.

The study also showed that waist circumference, which indicates abdominal obesity, may be linked to cancer risk that is similar to that of individuals with overweight.

The study researchers used the thresholds set out by the Korean Society for the Study of Obesity. These thresholds put the waist circumference cutoff at over 90 cm (35.4 in) for males and over 85cm (33.46 in) for females.

These are not universal cutoffs. According to the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI), waist circumference measurements that can increase your risk of negative health issues are 101.6 cm (40 in) for males and 88.9 cm (35 in) for females.

Previous research has also suggested an association between waist circumference and cancer risk, independent of BMI. One study showed a potential 11% increased risk of cancer in people with a waist circumference over the thresholds, even if they were physically active.

The current study found that males had a higher relative association between obesity and cancer, while females showed higher absolute risk.

The researchers also found that the absolute risk was higher in adults ages 30 to 39.

Those who currently smoke or who have ever smoked were also found to have a higher risk of developing cancer than those who have never smoked.

“Diet, exercise, and now medications can all be used very effectively to reduce one’s weight and, hopefully as a result, cancer risk,” Thanki said.

He also noted that, due to differences between South Korean populations and those in other countries such as the United States, further studies will be needed to determine how this translates across other populations.

“But I think this trend will likely extend across all cultures,” he said.

#4765. Cat-sized foxes in Texas are in trouble. Big guard dogs could help.

Published Nov 3, 2026 5:10 PM EST

Two guard dogs could be protecting more than just the livestock grazing on the Rita Blanca National Grasslands in the Texas Panhandle. The working canines may be helping increase the odds of survival for the Lone Star State’s smallest fox.

The swift fox (Vulpes velox) is about the size of a house cat. While not federally listed as endangered, conservationists believe there are fewer than 250 left in Texas. They only occupy about 40 percent of their historic range, from Texas north to Alberta, Canada.

“The swift fox relies on the shortgrass prairie ecosystem once found across the Panhandle and into western Texas,” Haley Sloan, a doctoral student at Texas A&M, said in a profile. “Coyotes can take advantage of the cover provided by the taller vegetation that has grown into these areas, resulting in coyote predation being a leading cause of mortality in swift fox populations.”

Sloan is currently studying if livestock guardian dogs paired with a cattle herd can reduce swift fox mortality. The thought is that the dogs will act as a larger predator, and change the way the coyotes behave and use their habitat.

“The hope is that the dogs’ presence will deter coyotes, thereby reducing swift fox mortality and allowing the foxes to start using areas where the coyotes are being excluded,” Sloan said.

The dogs work in northwestern Texas’ Dallam County, the only known county in the state that still has a swift fox population. The swift fox’s small size and diet of insects, plants, and small rodents also means that they don’t pose any threats to cattle, sheep, and goats.

If incorporating these livestock guardian dogs with cattle herds alters the coyotes’ behavior, Sloan said that it offers two potential benefits. It could improve the chances of swift fox survival, while reducing the threat of livestock predation, especially during the vulnerable calving season.

To monitor the animals’ behavior, Sloan and the other researchers put GPS collars on coyotes and swift foxes ahead of this three-year-long project. The livestock guardian dogs were introduced with the cattle herd this summer. While it is too early to report any initial findings, the team has high hopes.

“I’m happy to report right now the dogs are doing great,” Sloan said. “The producer involved in the project hasn’t lost any calves to predation, and I have hope we’ll have similar positive outcomes for swift foxes in the vicinity of the herd.”

#4763. Yamaha unveils new NMAX E, bringing electric power to its popular motorbike lineup

Yamaha is expanding its electric two-wheeler lineup with a much more capable machine, unveiling the new NMAX E as an electric version of its popular NMAX sport scooter.

The 2027 Yamaha NMAX E is being positioned as a 125cc-equivalent electric scooter, putting it firmly above the low-speed urban electric scooters that have made up much of Yamaha’s electric lineup thus far.

At its heart is Yamaha’s new compact eAxle drive unit, which sends power to the rear wheel through a belt drive. The electric motor produces 6.7 kW (9 hp) of nominal power and peaks at 7.5 kW (10 hp), along with 33.3 Nm (24.6 lb-ft) of torque.

Yamaha hasn’t published a top speed in the specifications, but the NMAX E’s A1 classification puts it in the same general category as 125cc combustion scooters rather than urban mopeds.

Power comes from a centrally mounted 3.5 kWh lithium-ion battery, which Yamaha says provides up to 104 km (65 miles) of range on the WMTC Class 1 testing cycle. The L-shaped battery is mounted low and centrally in the chassis to help maintain a low center of gravity.

Unlike many electric scooters that rely on removable batteries, the NMAX E uses a fixed pack. Yamaha has compensated for that with an onboard 800W charger, allowing riders to plug the scooter directly into a household outlet or an AC Type 2 public charging station. A full 0-100% charge takes around 5.5 hours.

Riders can choose between three riding modes. Sport (S) mode offers the quickest acceleration, Touring (T) provides smoother power delivery for everyday riding and carrying a passenger, and Eco (E) reduces acceleration and top speed while maximizing range. Regenerative braking is also included.

The rest of the scooter is fairly well equipped, including traction control, ABS, 245mm front and rear disc brakes, 13-inch wheels, a 33mm fork, dual rear shocks, and even a reverse mode to make low-speed maneuvering easier.

Nice, the Nmax has always been the premium scoot we try to get when traveling in southeast asia. Always felt like it would've been even better electrified. No removable battery seems a bit of a miss. That might constrain a big chunk of demand.

A five-inch TFT display includes smartphone connectivity through Yamaha’s Motor On app, providing turn-by-turn navigation as well as battery status, ride information, maintenance reminders, and other connected features. There’s also keyless ignition, USB-C charging, LED lighting, and illuminated underseat storage large enough for a full-face helmet, depending on its size.

Perhaps most importantly, the NMAX E looks like a proper Yamaha scooter rather than an electric experiment. Its dual headlights and distinctive side panels closely follow the styling language of Yamaha’s existing MAX family.

That could prove important as established motorcycle manufacturers increasingly attempt to bring electric models into their existing lineups rather than treating them as separate curiosities.

Pricing and exact market availability haven’t yet been announced, but Yamaha is positioning the NMAX E as a 2027 model for the European market.

#4762. Maladaptive Daydreaming and ADHD

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 12, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley

One of the greatest things about the internet is finding out you’re not alone. I feel sorry for those Victorian souls who had a weird thought and simply had to live with it. Instead of going on Reddit and searching, “Does anyone else pretend to be a chicken to get to sleep at night?” they sat there in their little nightcaps by candlelight, feeling like the biggest weirdos on Earth, when they could have been doomscrolling for three hours about how many people had the exact same fantasy and, even more comforting, even weirder and more bizarre ones. Which brings me to my most recent discovery. It not only made me feel less of an oddball, but it also gave me that now-familiar feeling: Has anyone on this planet ever had a truly unique experience?

According to subreddit threads, no. We are all infinitely bizarre and confused creatures, bumbling around and trying to look like we’ve got our sh*t together when we clearly don’t. That brings me a great deal of comfort, knowing I’m not alone.

As a woman with ADHD, I’ve spent my life feeling like an alien who has landed on Earth while everyone else received the manual on how to be human except me. It turns out that even that alien feeling is common among people with ADHD. Through my research into women with ADHD, I keep finding stories I thought were as odd and unique as that chicken dream, only to discover they’re not.

One of the most shameful aspects of ADHD for many of us is how much of our mental landscape is taken up by living in entirely fictional versions of our lives. Some of these are so vivid that they intermingle with reality, and it becomes hard to tell the real life from the fantasy. This might seem like a very strange concept to a neurotypical person, but many ADHDers will resonate with it on several levels. I used to do it so much that I truly didn’t realise it was a thing. I thought everyone lived in a parallel universe of epic proportions.

This is known as maladaptive daydreaming (MD), a proposed condition in which someone gets absorbed in vivid, story-like fantasy for so long that it takes over their life. The term was coined in 2002 by Eli Somer of the University of Haifa, who described it as extensive fantasy activity that replaces human interaction or interferes with academic, interpersonal, or vocational functioning (Somer, 2002). The fantasies usually have characters, plots, and settings, and people with MD can tell their fantasies aren’t real, which separates it from psychosis. It isn’t an official diagnosis, but as researchers like myself uncover more about the lived experiences of people with ADHD, it appears to be especially common in this population (Somer et al., 2017; Theodor-Katz et al., 2022).

What is it about ADHD that makes maladaptive daydreaming so appealing? From my own anecdotal research, it can be a form of escape from a world that often feels unkind and full of rejection. From early childhood, many people with ADHD experience increased levels of bullying and negative feedback because of their behaviour (Abregú-Crespo et al., 2024; Becker et al., 2017), which can create deeply felt low self-esteem and a sense of unworthiness. One way of coping can be to escape into a fantasy of “One day…I’ll show them all!”

There is something about the ADHD mind that tends to wander off into other dimensions, but when it does, what are the most common fantasies people engage in? Getting people to open up about the innermost workings of their minds is notoriously difficult, even in non-judgmental research settings, but a quick subreddit search throws up some revealing insights. Nowacki and Pyszkowska (2024) found that Reddit users described fantasies about being a perfect version of themselves, undoing past mistakes, and having imagined companions who offer constant support. Others imagined being a confident leader, the opposite of their real-life selves, or went back to painful memories to have their younger selves rescued. One poster dated the start of their excessive daydreaming to being bullied by siblings. While these accounts are not specific to ADHD, they show how fantasy can serve as both comfort and escape from a world that feels unforgiving.

So if your mind is off in another universe right now, don’t beat yourself up. You’re in very good company, and with a little kindness you can enjoy the daydreams without letting them run the show. In my book of ADHD hacks, How to Get Your Sh*t Together, I devote a whole chapter to forgiving yourself and all your ADHD quirks, and daydreaming is just one of them (Murphy, [2026]).

Murphy, B. (2026). How to get your sh*t together [Kindle ebook].

Abregú-Crespo, R., Garriz-Luis, A., et al. (2024). School bullying in children and adolescents with neurodevelopmental and psychiatric conditions: A systematic review and meta-analysis. The Lancet Child & Adolescent Health, 8(2), 122–134. doi.org/10.1016/S2352-4642(23)00289-4

Becker, S. P., Mehari, K. R., Langberg, J. M., & Evans, S. W. (2017). Rates of peer victimization in young adolescents with ADHD and associations with internalizing symptoms and self-esteem. European Child & Adolescent Psychiatry, 26(2), 201–214. doi.org/10.1007/s00787-016-0881-y

Nowacki, A., & Pyszkowska, A. (2024). The everchanging maladaptive daydreaming: A thematic analysis of lived experiences of Reddit users. Current Psychology, 43, 28488–28499. doi.org/10.1007/s12144-024-06506-3

Somer, E. (2002). Maladaptive daydreaming: A qualitative inquiry. Journal of Contemporary Psychotherapy, 32(2), 197–212. doi.org/10.1023/A:1020597026919

Somer, E., Soffer-Dudek, N., & Ross, C. A. (2017). The comorbidity of daydreaming disorder (maladaptive daydreaming). The Journal of Nervous and Mental Disease, 205(7), 525–530. doi.org/10.1097/NMD.0000000000000685

Theodor-Katz, N., Somer, E., Hesseg, R. M., & Soffer-Dudek, N. (2022). Could immersive daydreaming underlie a deficit in attention? The prevalence and characteristics of maladaptive daydreaming in individuals with ADHD. Journal of Clinical Psychology, 78(11).

#4761. Want to become a creative genius? Try this nap hack.

Published Nov 4, 2026 8:30 AM EST

What’s the weirdest thing you learned this week? Well, whatever it is, we promise you’ll have an even weirder answer if you listen to PopSci’s hit podcast. The Weirdest Thing I Learned This Week hits Spotify, YouTube, Apple, and everywhere else you listen to podcasts every-other Wednesday morning. It’s your new favorite source for the strangest science-adjacent facts, figures, and Wikipedia spirals the editors of Popular Science can muster. If you like the stories in this post, we guarantee you’ll love the show.

The internet insists that Edison, Tesla, Einstein, Da Vinci, and Dalí all shared this own cool hack: they napped while holding something heavy, so the clatter would wake them mid-dream and they could grab hold of their unconscious musings before they evaporated. I could only really find a direct source linking such practices to one of them: Dalí. But modern science suggests he may have been on to something.

In 50 Secrets of Magic Craftsmanship, the artist describes “slumber with a key,” which involves a bony Spanish-style armchair, a heavy key, and a plate on the floor. When the key slips out of your fingers and clangs, you wake up. According to Dalí, just a few seconds of slumber could yield priceless creative insights.

There’s some real neuroscience behind this silly-sounding practice, and it comes down to something now known as N1 sleep. As you fall asleep, you pass through N1, the lightest stage of non-REM sleep, where your muscles relax and your brain starts producing dreamlike imagery drawn from your recent experiences. People woken from N1 often swear they were never asleep, yet “microdreams” from these brief siestas can cram elaborate scenes into a few seconds.

Researchers got curious about whether that loose, wandering state could boost creativity. They started with narcolepsy, a condition that involves frequent slips between wake and sleep. They compared 185 patients to 126 typical sleepers and found the narcoleptics scored higher on every creativity measure. The more hybrid-state symptoms they had, the higher the score.

Then, with a strong hunch that this in-between phase could be the key to creativity, they tested N1’s impact directly. Participants worked through a math task with a hidden shortcut, and those who hadn’t found it after 30 rounds took a 20-minute break in a dark room holding a plastic bottle. If they fell asleep and dropped the bottle, they would wake up. Of the 24 who dropped it after reaching N1, 20 (83 percent) found the trick afterward, compared with 15 of 59 (30%) who stayed awake. Even 15 seconds in N1 helped, but dozing deeper erased the benefit.

But unlike Dalí’s reported experiences, people didn’t emerge from N1 with a brilliant idea in tow. The nappers took an average of 94 more trials to crack the math problem. It’s not like they spent their nap time actively working on the math either: the content of their reported N1 dreams had no bearing on how quickly they solved the problem. The link between an N1 wake-up and boosted brainpower was squishier than that, which feels kind of spooky. Listen to this week’s episode to hear more about why we do our best creative work when rudely awoken—and how researchers at MIT are trying to harness this hack.

This week’s episode featured special guest Adam Conover of Adam Ruins Everything fame. He joined the show to talk about some surprising figures on male sexuality that he learned while working on his new comedy special, Big Divorce Energy.

You probably wouldn’t be surprised to hear that more than half of women surveyed admit to having faked an orgasm at some point, given how often those performances are referenced in TV shows and movies. But research consistently shows that men fake orgasms, too. One study found that around a quarter of men reported doing so.

Adam certainly found that stat surprising, and he’s spent a lot of time thinking about why—and going down rabbit holes about what other aspects of straight, male sexuality get taken for granted. If men aren’t willing to talk about the orgasms they fake, what else are they sweeping under the rug? Check out this week’s episode for more.

There’ve been dozens of reported cases of spontaneous human combustion throughout history, going as far back as 17th Century Europe and as recently as 2010, when 76-year-old Michael Faherty’s death in Galway, Ireland, sparked talk of this spooky phenomenon.

One famous 1731 account of Countess Cornelia Bandi’s untimely demise, written by a priest, Giuseppe Bianchini, is particularly harrowing. It describes just a few blackened bits and body parts remaining, amid the apparent and mysterious destruction of most of her body. Her lower legs allegedly remained intact (stockings and all!) while the rest was burned to greasy ash. It’s not surprising that Giuseppe’s tale took on a life of its own. After all, getting reduced to a pile of cinders and a pair of ankles is quite the way to go.

Famous authors, starting with Charles Dickens in Bleak House, took inspiration from these startling descriptions, which popped up in Enlightenment and Victorian-era tabloids. And Dickens, in particular, latched onto the idea—taking it as 100% fact that a human being could erupt in flames with no particular outside interference. In fact, Dickens was one half of a 10-month long, public debate about whether or not spontaneous human combustion is possible. Dickens and his friend, philosopher George Lewes, had a major disagreement over the science in the form of back and forth published letters and installments of Bleak House, where Dickens would routinely defend spontaneous human combustion in the introduction to each chapter.

Since Dickens helped to popularize and defend the phenomenon, it’s stayed persistent among a certain set of conspiracy theorists and pseudoscientists. There are lots of ideas about how and why a person might suddenly burst into flames out there, from lightning strikes, intestinal gases, acts of God, and even ketosis. But the truth is likely a little sadder, if not stranger.

The prevailing scientific wisdom suggests most of these mysterious deaths are the outcome of the “wick effect.” Under the right conditions, some people basically burn like candles. Thanks to experiments with pig carcasses, blankets, and one woman’s osteoporitic bones at the Tennessee Body Farm, we know that an elderly person wearing the wrong clothes at the wrong time near an open flame can unfortunately burn long enough and hot enough to destroy most of a body, bone and all, without necessarily igniting a house fire.

#4760. Maximo milestone: friendly robot has completed 300,000 tasks

After completing the first half of Amazon’s Bellefield complex last summer, Maximo engineers have put their helpful robot friend into high gear, with the latest version 3.0 robot-equipped construction crews installing as many as 24 solar panel modules per hour, per person. And now, the company is reporting that Maximo has completed its 300,000th construction task. (!)

If that 24 modules per hour, per person rate sounds fast, that’s because it is. At full tilt, the latest Maximo robot-equipped crews have nearly doubled the output of traditional installation methods at similar solar locations throughout Southern California. Now, with 300,000 tasks under its belt, the robot is proving to be both fast and durable.

“The future of solar construction depends on bringing together the experience of our people and new technology,” explains Matt Tetrault, President of Primoris’ Renewables business.

Like just about everyone these days, Maximo is playing up its machines’ NVDIVIA hardware, re-branding its robots’ repetitive automation as “physical AI.” That’s not to say the robots don’t work, however – as their deployment at Amazon’s Bellefield solar field is proving.

(By) leveraging NVIDIA AI infrastructure together with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries and NVIDIA Isaac Sim open robotics simulation framework, the Maximo team was able to develop, test and refine robotic capabilities through physics-based simulation and AI driven modeling before deploying updates in the field. The combination of AI, vision, robotics and simulation driven engineering reduced development and validation timelines and increased confidence in field performance as the robotic fleet scaled.

Amazon Web Services (AWS) powered the development, deployment, and operation of Maximo’s AI-driven field systems. AWS provides scalable computing, automated software delivery, and advanced data analytics, including real-time construction intelligence, enabling Maximo to collect operational robotics data and continuously improve performance.

The rapid deployment of solar panels at utility scale projects like this one, which is set to eventually reach over a GW of solar generating capacity, will help companies like Amazon reduce their carbon footprint, of course – but also save them big money as the price of fossil fuels continues to climb.

So Primoris’ Renewables is the name of a business, Maximo is the name of a solar robotics company incubated by The AES Corporation. Maximo makes a robot (also called Maximo I think) using NVDIVIA hardware and software, and also AWS cloud software, and Bellefield is a solar field owned by Amazon. Or so I gather so far.

The Maximo team says it has plans to extend its robots potential use cases beyond solar and into construction tasks that require similar pick and place and feeding and attaching movements, site logistics, and site cleanup. And like just about every other business that demands a high degree of physical labor, the construction industry is facing huge labor shortages, making machines like Maximo that provide real efficiency gains welcome additions to the job site.

#4759. The Utter Predictability of the Nvidia/Jensen Huang Debacle

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 12, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley

It’s not every day that an email makes international news before toppling global stock markets and beheading the organizational chart of one of tech's household names. But if you’re Jensen Huang admitting to at least one extramarital affair to all 40,000+ employees of Nvidia, this all makes too much sense.

Since the story broke about the married-with-children billionaire CEO behind the world’s most powerful AI company sleeping with not only an alleged Chinese spy, but also an employee, the internet has gone giddy with memes, commentary, and endless speculation about what goes on inside closed rooms–bedrooms and boardrooms alike. I’ll leave the economists to make predictions about the future of the AI market without its most famous CEO at the helm and politicians to quibble about what this means for U.S.-China ties going forward. As a psychologist, though, I think now is a good time to revisit the long-established predictors of marital fidelity, which is less of a black box and more of a formula.

Much investigative journalism has gone into the dark and mysterious convergence of events leading to Huang meeting and subsequently falling for Alice Huang, the presumed Chinese operative, as well as the more quotidian circumstances that led to his affair with Kimberly Powell, his executive and subordinate. But as much as extenuating situations can promote infidelity, personality matters too.

A while back, researchers conducted a series of studies to show just how well a person’s humility and honesty predicted their capacity to lie in their romantic relationships. Tech billionaires are known for many things, but humility is not one of them. Curiously, the research on humility and relationship dishonesty also found that proud/dishonest people should also be more likely to suspect their relationship partners’ dishonesty (thanks to our tendency to project ourselves onto others). But in the Jensen case, he did appear to defy this trend when he failed to be suspicious of his spy-mistress.

Of course, the personality traits that made Jensen into both a billionaire and a bad husband are only part of the equation. The situation always matters, and the link between power and cheating has long been established. Time and again, studies have shown that people who naturally have more power or are temporarily made to feel more powerful are more likely to cheat on their relationship partners.

While this trend is in part because power makes you more impulsive, likely to act, self-focused, and psychologically distant from other people, it’s also moderated by beliefs. Because people like to validate themselves, power seems to have these negative effects on relationship fidelity only when the person has positive thoughts about cheating. For those who think of cheating negatively, power doesn’t make them more likely to be unfaithful.

Money has a similar effect. In one study, men who were made to feel richer were less satisfied with their partner’s physical attractiveness and more likely to approach an attractive woman. Other research has found that being extremely financially focused in general predicts worse relationship satisfaction.

There is at least one more layer to the latest Nvidia scandal: the organizational context. A researcher once called affairs an “occupational hazard” because they were more likely in some organizations than others. Relative to people in other jobs, those in higher administrative positions and in technology were the least likely to say sex with someone other than your spouse was always wrong. This is also consistent with findings from the dating site for married people interested in affairs, AshleyMadison.com, showing that the top industry for their users was IT and Engineering.

Finally, something has to be said about the fact that the Jensen affairs have been years in the making, and the fact that the world is only finding out about it now suggests collusion has been happening this whole time. Psychologists call this collective cheating. While the original work on collective cheating focused on other forms of dishonesty rather than the relational kind, the idea was the same: Sometimes our concern for the group makes us turn a blind eye, and that is at least part of the problem.

Abzug, R. (2016). Extramarital affairs as occupational hazard: A structural, ethical (cultural) model of opportunity. Sexualities, 19(1-2), 25-45.

Lamprinakos, G., Santos, D., Stavraki, M., Brinol, P., Magrizos, S., & Petty, R. E. (2024). Power can increase but also decrease cheating depending on what thoughts are validated. Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 111, 104578.

#4758. Relaxed bear wins award for luxurious eating style—underneath an Alaskan waterfall

Published Nov 4, 2026 11:13 AM EST

Typically, when a bear catches a nutritious salmon, they don’t eat it under a rushing waterfall. But one unnamed black bear (Ursus americanus) eating at Anan Creek in Alaska’s Tongass National Forest decided to park underneath a waterfall and enjoy his fishy snack.

For this culinary innovation, the U.S. Forest Service team at Tongass National Forest has awarded the unnamed bear with the 2026 Shower Beer award.

“After watching this relaxed black bear gnawing on a salmon under rushing waters, we’re wondering if it might catch on—like the ursine equivalent of the shower beer,” the team writes. “The more you watch, the more sense it makes. No mess and no need to move to start fishing again. This bear may be on to something.”

The rangers at Tongass National Forest are currently awarding the Anan Bear Awards to the 39 bears spotted at the Anan Wildlife Observatory over the summer.

Tongass is the largest national forest in the United States, and covers most of southeastern Alaska, including the capital city of Juneau. The area includes Mendanhall Glacier (a popular destination for Alaskan cruises), hiking trails, eagles soaring above, and plenty of bears. One of the hotspots is Anan Creek, home to one of the largest runs of pink salmon in Southeast Alaska.

According to Friends of Anan, 39 bears are known to feast on the salmon at Anan Creek. The population includes 31 black bears and eight brown bears (Ursus arctos). Like their beefy counterparts farther to the north in Katmai National Park, the bears return annually each summer to eat salmon and teach their cubs how to fish and survive. And also like the fat bears of Katmai, every bear here has their own habits and quirks.

The U.S. Forest Service tracks and documents every bear spotted here, while explore.org’s cameras broadcast live streams of their behavior.

#4757. Former CAKE team is back in the kitchen with a new electric motorcycle

If the new ReBake Abler electric motorcycle looks like it might share a bit of DNA with Sweden’s dearly departed CAKE, there’s a good reason for that.

ReBake Motors has officially unveiled its first electric two-wheeler at EICMA 2026 in Milan, introducing the Abler as a highly modular, utility-focused electric moped and light motorcycle.

Behind the new Swedish company is founder and CEO Karl Ytterborn, who spent eight years at CAKE from its founding in 2016 through 2024. CAKE famously built some of the most interesting minimalist electric motorcycles and utility bikes on the market before ultimately collapsing after failing to secure additional funding. Ytterborn says ReBake is intended to apply many of the lessons learned during that experience, while eliminating unnecessary cost and complexity.

Its chunky 42mm aluminum tube frame isn’t just a styling exercise. ReBake designed it as a mounting system, allowing cargo accessories to attach directly to the frame at multiple locations. That means riders can configure the bike for everything from carrying groceries and passengers to more serious utility duties.

There are two versions. The Abler45 is an EU L1e-B moped with a 45 km/h (28 mph) top speed, 4 kW nominal motor and 5.12 kW peak output. It starts at €3,990 including VAT.

The €4,990 Abler80 steps up to the A1 light motorcycle category, increasing nominal power to 6.14 kW and peak power to 7.68 kW while pushing the top speed beyond 80 km/h (50 mph). Both versions use a direct-drive rear hub motor.

Energy comes from removable 2 kWh lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries weighing 17 kg (37.5 lb) apiece. The Abler45 comes standard with one battery but can carry two, while the Abler80 includes two for 4 kWh of total capacity. With both batteries, ReBake claims up to 160 km (99 miles) of low-speed urban range on the Abler45 or 114 km (71 miles) on the Abler80. Each battery can be charged either on or off the bike from a normal 230V outlet, reaching a full charge in four hours.

The rest of the hardware includes 14-inch cast wheels, 140mm of front suspension travel, dual rear shocks, front and rear disc brakes with combined braking, regenerative braking, and full LED lighting.

Perhaps more interesting than any individual specification, though, is simply seeing another Swedish electric motorcycle startup emerge from CAKE’s ashes.

CAKE demonstrated that there was plenty of appetite for unconventional, lightweight electric motorcycles. Unfortunately, it also demonstrated just how difficult it is to turn that enthusiasm into a sustainable business.

ReBake appears to be getting another crack at that equation – this time with eight years’ worth of lessons already baked in.

#4756. Mental Health Care Has a Time Problem

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 12, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley

We tell people to make time for their mental health as if time were theirs to make.

For someone paid by the hour, a therapy appointment can cost wages as well as a copay. For a parent or caregiver, getting help may require arranging care for someone else first. Even when treatment is technically available, it may not be available when we can actually use it.

The World Health Organization is asking that people’s lived experiences shape mental health services. We could start by taking seriously an experience that is easy to mistake for an excuse: “I don’t have time.”

The latest National Survey on Drug Use and Health, released in July, found that 49.1 percent of American adults with mental illness received no mental health treatment in 2025. Among untreated adults who felt they needed care, 48.3 percent said they did not have enough time. Cost was an even more common barrier (61.4 percent).

We need policies that protect time for mental health care. But what are people supposed to do while those protections remain out of reach, or when care isn’t available?

My interest in that question began at Plum Village, a mindfulness practice center founded by Thích Nhất Hạnh. During a stay there, I proudly told a monk named Brother Treasure that I’d just meditated for three hours.

He smiled, “How about three breaths? That’s all that you need to tune into the present moment.”

I was so embarrassed. But that exchange helped shape my research as a psychologist: What if well-being didn’t have to compete with the rest of our lives for time?

At Berkeley, my colleagues and I studied an exercise called self-compassionate touch: resting your hands over your heart and belly while responding to yourself with a kind inner voice. We randomly assigned 135 college students to practice either this exercise or a finger-tapping control group for 20 seconds a day for a month.

Compared to daily finger-tapping, just 20 seconds a day of self-compassionate touch was associated with greater improvements in self-compassion, stress, and mental health. The effects were comparable in size to those found in much more time-intensive interventions.

I call practices like these micropractices. They take 30 seconds or less, or can be woven into something you’re already doing. Noticing your footsteps on the way to the bus. Taking three slow, deep breaths before opening your inbox. Doing a yoga pose between tasks.

Although we extended this research on 20-second self-compassionate touch in a six-month study of 497 U.S. adults, published last month, my research alone can’t tell us how broadly this idea applies. But as I started looking beyond my own research, I found further evidence that practices can have measurable effects in seconds. In a separate experiment, another research group found that 20 seconds of self-soothing touch reduced the stress hormone cortisol following a stressful experience. And recent studies show that 30 seconds of slow, deep breathing can reduce anxiety, slow heart rate, and increase alpha and theta brain-wave activity associated with calm and focused attention.

More broadly, I kept running into studies that challenged an assumption I had largely taken for granted: that more time means more benefit.

An analysis of 203 randomized controlled trials on meditation found duration of sessions wasn’t associated with better mental health outcomes.

A study of 21,088 mindfulness app users objectively tracked session duration and frequency. The pattern was similar: Consistent practice was associated with reduced stress; longer sessions were not.

And it’s not just meditation. In an analysis of 137 trials of touch interventions and practices involving 12,966 people, more sessions were associated with better mental health outcomes. But longer sessions? No extra benefit. In fact, when it came to lowering cortisol, and even reducing blood pressure, longer sessions were less effective than shorter ones.

Breathwork points in the same direction. An analysis of 12 randomized controlled trials of breathwork interventions (like slow deep breathing) totaling 785 adults found that reductions in stress were not associated with session length.

And sometimes, breaking the same amount of movement into smaller pieces can be more beneficial than doing it all at once. In one study, six five-minute walks spread across the day improved mood, fatigue, and food cravings more than a single 30-minute walk.

None of this means that 30 seconds is always enough, or that longer practices have no value. But many of us only have a 30-second window—or at least a lot more of them: between Zoom meetings, in the checkout line, at a red light, or while waiting for the microwave to ring. And if the choice is between 30 seconds and nothing at all, I’d bet on 30 seconds.

The point is not that complex suffering has a 30-second solution. Nor is this a substitute for psychotherapy, medication, or any longer practice that is already helping. It’s more like brushing your teeth: It doesn’t replace the dentist, but it helps you keep things in check. In the same way, these tiny practices can give you a way of not being left empty-handed when the system isn’t there.

Lack of time, however, isn’t merely a personal problem.

A 2024 study found that after states adopted paid-sick-leave mandates, Medicaid-financed prescriptions for mental health conditions increased by about 6 percent per year. Protecting people’s time can help them use care. And we can also design forms of support that demand less of that time. These aren’t competing approaches. We need both.

Institutions need to do more than tell us to take care of ourselves. A company that offers employees a breathing exercise should protect time to attend a therapy appointment. A health system that offers a self-guided resource should provide a clear route to a clinician.

The best self-help doesn’t teach people that they should be able to handle everything themselves. It creates more moments in which help is possible while leaving the door open to more.

We need to move beyond reminding people that their mental health matters. We need to take “I don’t have time” seriously. People deserve care that fits the lives they actually have. Sometimes that means systems that protect an hour for therapy. Sometimes it means discovering that a meaningful practice doesn’t require another hour, or even another minute.

It can begin with 30 seconds you already have.

#4755. Man builds robotic cat feeder that senses when dish is empty

Published Nov 4, 2026 12:00 PM EST

Pet owners can pick from any number of automatic cat feeders at this point, and even shell out hundreds of dollars for a particularly fancy kit. But at the end of the day, most of them are simply a scooper that dumps out premeasured amounts of feline food based on an internal timer.

Jason Winfield, a New Zealand-based YouTuber and frequent traveler, wanted a slightly more advanced option: a robotic cat feeder that distributes a predetermined amount of food for his two pals, and also senses when the dish is actually empty.

“I tried a few of those automatic feeders off-the-shelf, and look, they’re fine. They do the job. Sort of,” Winfield explains in his recent video. “But here’s what bothered me: How do I know my cat actually ate?”

Winfield’s invention is designed to avoid overfeeding or accidentally building a mountain of kibble. The device runs on a Raspberry Pi Pico with Wi-Fi capabilities, and includes a tiny LCD screen and a buzzer to alert when food has been delivered. An onboard real-time clock (RTC) module keeps time even without direct power, which allows for a timed feeding window for daily rations.

Winfield also attached a 3D-printed cat head toggle to cycle through settings on the feeder’s screen. DIY projects like this are bound to run into errors, so Winfield also encoded a failsafe that turns off the feed dispenser if the dish has remained full for a specific length of time.There’s even an ultrasonic sensor to detect the presence of a cat, so the feeder doesn’t inadvertently drop kibble on their head.

The end result is an efficient, reliable automatic feeder that keeps Winfield’s cats happy. Winfield himself is even confident that his cats will never go hungry while he’s traveling.

#4754. Letter From the Editor-in-Chief: What a Decade of Bedtime Stories Taught Me About Health

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

I’ve read to my children each night at bedtime for as long as I (and they) can remember. We started with the likes of “Goodnight Batcave” and the lesser-known-in-the-US but oh-so-wonderful collection of verse-driven classics from former UK Children’s Laureate Julia Donaldson.

We moved on to B.J. Novak’s anarchic love letter to the power of words (and to great typography), “The Book With No Pictures.”

We eventually worked our way up to Roald Dahl’s wickedly dark back catalog, discovering more complex characters, language and plotting as we went.

When my eldest, Amelia, hit 6, it was time to roll out the big guns.

Over the last 5 years (she’s now 11), I’ve read the seven Harry Potter books aloud twice, complete with all the voices: once to Amelia on her own, once to both her and her brother, Henry, two years her junior.

I had feared she wouldn’t be keen on another helping, but Amelia immersed herself once more in the world of Hogwarts with no hesitation and took immense joy in watching Henry discover for himself every twist and turn on Harry’s journey.

We have done the same thing with Tolkien’s “The Hobbit” and his fantasy masterpiece “The Lord of the Rings,” and are currently midway through “The Two Towers” on our second go around.

There’s a huge amount of reciprocal joy we take from this nightly ritual, beyond the practical benefits of providing a calming demarcation between the end of the day and the wind-down to sleep.

For me, it comes as either a break in my working day or a signal that it’s over, depending on how hectic things are.

For the kids, it’s an all-too-rare chance to get me all to themselves, no deadlines, screens, or other distractions to pull me away from being anything but 100% present.

For all three of us, it’s a literal (and literary!) warm blanket — a chance to escape under the covers to familiar worlds and familiar faces. It is, in short, incredibly good for our well-being.

And yet, in the world of health information — including on this site — thousands, if not millions, of reading hours are dedicated to the benefits of nutrition, sleep, and exercise as the building blocks of good health. Reading itself rarely makes that shortlist.

For me, it unequivocally deserves a place on it. Research seems to support that case. Even if we need more of it to really understand how and why.

A recent editorial in Psychological Medicine co-authored by Barbara Sahakian, Professor of Clinical Neuropsychology at Cambridge University, draws on a broad range of research linking reading for pleasure to better mental health and greater empathy.

The positive impact of reading on young people — just like Amelia and Henry — also carries evidence.

Among more than 10,000 US adolescents, those who started reading for pleasure early had fewer mental health problems, spent less time on screens and slept more. Although, per an earlier column of mine, I can’t vouch for the sleep side of things when it comes to early bird Henry.

For many, reading can be a form of therapy that improves well-being. Bibliotherapy is a complementary therapeutic tool for emotional release and reduced stress and anxiety, with its roots traced back to ancient civilizations.

There’s even research suggesting a link between a love of reading and a lower risk of cognitive decline.

In a 2003 study of people aged 75 and over, reading was associated with a 35% lower risk of dementia over roughly five years.

A separate 14-year study from 2022 found that people who read at least weekly saw less cognitive decline, whatever their level of education.

A happy (and healthy) by-product of this love of being read to is that both my kids have now started reading to me at bedtime. Henry recently read “Jeffy the Burglar’s Cat” to us, a lesser-known but no less compelling chapter book by Ursula Moray Williams that was a staple of my own childhood. And we’ve enjoyed several books from Amelia, including the wistful tale of friendship and the circle of life, “Charlotte’s Web” by E.B. White – not a dry eye in the house for the final few chapters of that one.

They’ve also gone off and re-read the Harry Potter books and “The Hobbit” to themselves.

The research above links reading to many health benefits: better attention and memory, fewer mental health problems, more sleep, less time on screens, and greater empathy. I haven’t measured any of those impacts empirically in our house. Nor am I naive to the fact that as they get older, they’ll ultimately grow out of me reading to them, with school, extracurricular activities, their friends, and inevitably screens competing for more and more of their time.

Come what may, though, I know that a child who considers missing a reading session as the most cardinal of cardinal sins, and who scrambles for the chance to read aloud to their dad at bedtime is, at that moment, concentrating, empathizing, discovering and growing.

Researchers are clear that studies espousing the benefits of reading show association rather than proof, and it’s evident that more experimental work and deeper research are needed to ensure the complex cause and effect stands on firm scientific ground.

Regardless, it’s a healthy habit Amelia, Henry and I are very happy to keep, and with a bit of luck, I’ll get to pass it on to their kids one day.

#4753. Tesla wins trade zone status for Texas Megapacks, but China tariffs stay

Tesla’s Megapack factory in Brookshire, Texas, is now officially a foreign-trade zone, a US customs program that lets manufacturers defer duties on imported parts. The FTZ Board’s approval, published in the Federal Register on Monday, runs for 14 months.

It’s easy to read this as Tesla getting a pass on tariffs for the Chinese LFP cells inside its Megapacks. Tesla’s own application says otherwise: parts hit by Section 301, 232, or 122 tariffs still pay them.

Tesla filed the request on May 20 for Subzone 84AM, part of FTZ 84 in the Houston area. That’s the factory where Tesla started Megapack 3 production in August, with a planned capacity of 50 GWh per year.

The application lists roughly 80 imported components Tesla wants to bring in under zone procedures, from coolant pumps and transformers to busbars, wiring harnesses, circuit boards and battery cells. Duty rates on those parts go up to 6.5%, while finished Megapacks and Bento inverters range from duty-free to 3.4%.

That gap is the usual reason companies set up an FTZ. A manufacturer in a zone can normally elect to pay the finished product’s lower rate instead of the rate on each imported part.

But the application spells out the limit. Components subject to duties under Section 122 of the Trade Act, Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act, or Section 301 “require subject merchandise to be admitted to FTZs in privileged foreign status,” according to the notice.

Privileged foreign status locks in a part’s own classification and tariff treatment when it enters the zone. So a Chinese LFP cell that ends up in a Megapack sold in the US still pays the Section 301 tariff on Chinese non-EV lithium-ion batteries, which jumped from 7.5% to 25% on January 1, 2026. Tesla just pays it later, when the finished Megapack leaves the zone.

Here’s what Tesla actually gets out of it:

The approval came with the same wording the FTZ Board has used all year. Production was “authorized on a limited basis,” and “further subject to a fourteen-month time period.”

Tesla got an identical decision for Megapack and inverter production at Fremont, Livermore and Lathrop in California this summer, with a one-year limit instead. Eastman Chemical, battery pack maker Rose Batteries, and chipmaker Qorvo all received similar time-limited, “limited basis” approvals in 2026.

The 14-month clock puts the expiry around the end of 2027. That’s roughly when LG Energy Solution is due to start supplying Tesla with LFP cells from Michigan under a $4.3 billion contract for Megapack 3, with mass production expected in the second half of 2027.

Tesla hasn’t hidden the issue. When tariffs escalated in April 2025, CFO Vaibhav Taneja said the impact on energy storage would be “outsized since we source lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery cells from China.” We wrote at the time that Tesla’s only growing business was kneecapped by Trump’s tariffs.

Tesla has since brought up its own LFP cell factory in Nevada, but Taneja said it would only cover a fraction of Tesla’s installed capacity. And Brookshire alone is designed for 50 GWh a year, on top of the 40 GWh Lathrop factory in California.

Tesla’s Megapacks are bringing big batteries to the grid, but you can get the same benefits at home by pairing solar with storage. With electricity rates up almost 10% last year and expected to keep climbing, going solar is one of the best ways to protect yourself against rising costs. #4752. Quieting Food Noise in Children

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 12, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley

Does your child seem to think about food all the time? You may find that they often ask when the next snack is, worry about whether they will get enough of a favorite food, sneak or hide food, or seem really focused on foods they often don’t get. Sometimes this is called food noise. Food noise is when a child finds themselves thinking about food a lot, even when they aren’t physically hungry. Many of us adults experience this as well, so we can relate to how our children feel and understand that it can be hard to reduce these thoughts.

As parents, our first reaction may be to set more limits. We may find ourselves hiding certain foods, locking cabinets, controlling portions, telling our child when they have had enough, or encouraging them to choose a “healthier” option. These responses come from a good place because we want our children to develop healthy eating habits in the long term. But sometimes, this control causes the food noise to get even louder.

A few strategies to help quiet this noise involve creating an environment around structure, trust, and food neutrality.

Kids do well when they know what to expect, and eating is no different. A regular meal and snack routine reassures children that another opportunity to eat is coming.

We recommend three meals and one to two planned snacks each day. Younger children might need an extra snack. The exact times will depend on school, activities, family schedules, and your child’s needs. Having this predictable routine helps children learn:

Posting the schedule for everyone to see in a centralized area, like on the pantry door or fridge, can be a good reminder.

If your child asks for food shortly after a meal or you catch them sneaking food at an unscheduled time, your role is to redirect them. Instead of saying, “You just ate! There is no way you can be hungry,” you might say:

Babies are born knowing how much they need to eat. They stop when they are full by pushing the bottle away and have telltale signs when they are hungry. Somewhere along the way, many kids stop listening to those hunger and fullness signals and begin relying on their parents and caregivers to decide how much they need.

This might look like encouraging them to take two more bites or finish everything on their plate and restricting how much they eat of more desirable foods when we feel like they are eating too much. This double-sided pressure often leads to children losing some of their ability to self-regulate their eating, which in turn leads to undereating or overeating at times.

Kids who become out of touch with these cues often have more food noise. When food feels scarce, they want it more. We encourage parents to let their children decide whether and how much they want to eat from what is provided at meals and snacks. When it becomes age-appropriate, we encourage children to make their own plates at meals. Parents can still serve hot foods if needed and ask the child how much they would like on their plate. This is not saying that they can eat as much as they want, whenever they want it. Not at all! It is saying that at the scheduled eating times, we want parents to step back and let kids take the lead in deciding how much they need to eat because only they know how hungry they are when they come to an eating time. Just like you and just like me.

At first, when children have this control, you may find that they will overeat. This is totally normal. They are learning, and it can take time for them to begin regulating on their own again. The important thing is to trust the process and keep practicing.

We often put foods into categories: good or bad, healthy or unhealthy. Kids pick up on these labels. When certain foods are placed on pedestals and others are treated as foods to avoid, it can have the opposite effect we intend. Kids become less interested in the food we call “healthy” and more interested in the foods we call "bad."

The take-home here is to avoid labeling food for yourself and when talking to your child. Kids are always listening to how we talk about food. Modeling simple, neutral food language helps them learn to see food without judgment or guilt.

Quieting food noise isn’t about teaching children to think less about food. It’s about creating an environment where they don’t have to think about it so much.

1. Skelton JA (2026). Your Child Is Not Their Weight. American Academy of Pediatrics.

2. American Academy of Pediatrics. Preschooler food and feeding. Healthy Active Living for Families. Accessed November 6, 2026.

4. Kleinman RE, Greer FR, eds. Pediatric Nutrition. 8th ed. American Academy of Pediatrics; 2020. doi:10.1542/9781610023610

#4751. EcoFlow’s new DELTA Gen4 portable power stations keep a reserve of extra power for emergencies

Published Nov 4, 2026 1:24 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn more ›

If you’ve ever driven with white knuckles to a gas station while your car’s range read “0 miles,” you’ll appreciate a new feature on this portable power station. EcoFlow is building a similar cushion into its new DELTA Gen4 portable power stations. A feature called Emergency Power Mode holds back a small reserve for charging phones after the screen hits 0 percent.

Two models are on sale today through EcoFlow’s website: the DELTA 3000 Gen4 at an early-bird $1,299 and the DELTA 3800 Gen4 at $1,699, against list prices of $1,699 and $2,199. Both put out 3,600 watts in chassis EcoFlow says are smaller and lighter than its DELTA 3 Ultra models, which include the DELTA 3 Ultra Plus we tried last year. They arrive a month after EcoFlow’s TITAN home batteries targeted whole-home backup.

A power station spends some charge just keeping its inverter awake. EcoFlow rates both DELTA Gen4 models at 14 watts with the AC outlets switched on and nothing plugged in, and 3 watts in standby. At 14 watts, a full day of idling uses 336 watt-hours, about 11 percent of the DELTA 3000 Gen4’s 3,072Wh battery.

The 3-watt standby number is what lets EcoFlow claim a fully charged DELTA 3800 Gen4 can sit for about 52 days before it drains, which matters for one parked in a closet waiting for an outage. EcoFlow pairs the lower overhead with a mode called Fridge Runtime Boost and rates the DELTA 3000 Gen4 for up to 58 hours of refrigerator runtime. The DELTA 3800 Gen4 gets more than 70 hours.

Those fridge numbers come from EcoFlow’s own tests with an empty 654-liter Samsung refrigerator, and the company notes that food load, room temperature, and door openings all change the result. The mode also supports one compressor-based appliance, such as a fridge or freezer, at a time, and EcoFlow says not to run other AC loads alongside it. We haven’t tested either DELTA Gen4 model yet, so these performance figures are EcoFlow’s. Emergency Power Mode covers what’s left after the battery runs down. You turn it on from the unit or the EcoFlow app, and EcoFlow says the reserve can give an iPhone 17 nearly a full extra charge.

Both DELTA Gen4 models share a 16.8 x 11.4-inch footprint, and both are rated for 3,600 watts continuous and 7,200 watts of surge from their 120V outlets. That’s enough to run a 1,500-watt space heater and a refrigerator at the same time with room to spare. EcoFlow’s original DELTA Pro weighed about 99 pounds to hit the same 3,600-watt rating.

The DELTA 3800 Gen4 fits 691 extra watt-hours and about 10 more pounds into the same footprint, for 3,763Wh at 67.5 pounds. EcoFlow says that’s roughly 33 pounds lighter than the DELTA Pro, and it holds slightly more energy. The DELTA 3000 Gen4 holds 3,072Wh at 57.3 pounds, and EcoFlow puts it at about 20 percent lighter than the DELTA 3 Ultra, with the same capacity.

The bigger model also has more ways to grow. The DELTA 3800 Gen4 takes up to 2,000 watts of solar across two inputs and has an expansion port for up to two extra batteries, including the DELTA Pro 3 Smart Extra Battery, for about 12kWh total. The DELTA 3000 Gen4 has one 1,000-watt solar input, and its spec sheet lists no battery port.

EcoFlow says the DELTA 3000 Gen4 refills from a wall outlet in under two hours and the DELTA 3800 Gen4 in under 2.5 hours. The 3kWh, 3,600-watt class is crowded, with Anker’s SOLIX F3000 and Jackery’s Explorer 3000 v2 at the same capacity and output. Our guide to the best portable power stations covers the field.

The DELTA 3000 Gen4 and DELTA 3800 Gen4 are listed for preorder. As of November 4, EcoFlow shows the DELTA 3800 Gen4 shipping in late November and the DELTA 3000 Gen4 in early December.

EcoFlow’s early-bird pricing runs through December 7. That puts the DELTA 3800 Gen4 at $1,699, 23 percent off its $2,199 list, and the DELTA 3000 Gen4 at $1,299, which is $400 below its $1,699 list.

For a house that needs a fridge, a router, and a few lamps through a weekend outage, this is the DELTA to look at first. It has the same 3,600-watt output as its bigger sibling and weighs about 10 pounds less. The savings come out of expandability, since it gets one 1,000-watt solar input, four charging methods, and no listed battery expansion.

At early-bird prices, $400 more buys 691 extra watt-hours, a second 1,000-watt solar input, and an expansion port that takes the system to about 12kWh with add-on batteries. That port is the reason to step up if you plan to expand a home-backup system later. EcoFlow rates it for more than 70 hours on a refrigerator and lists six ways to charge it.

#4749. Animal Play: From the Trash Can to Theories of Fairness

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 12, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley

I’ve been nose-deep in dog play for more than 50 years, and I never get bored. Dogs, like other animals, just want to have fun without a care in the world. These are some of my field notes from watching three dogs at play—Jethro, a large German shepherd/rottweiler/hound mutt; Zeke, a black lab; and Suki, a Belgian sheepdog:

Jethro runs toward Zeke, stops immediately in front of him, crouches on his forelimbs, wags his tail, barks, and immediately lunges, biting Zeke’s scruff and shaking his head rapidly from side to side. Jethro works his way around to his backside and mounts him, jumps off, does a rapid bow, lunges at his side and slams him with his hips, leaps up and bites his neck, and runs away. Zeke takes off in wild pursuit of Jethro, leaps on his back and bites his muzzle and scruff, then shakes his head rapidly from side to side. Suki bounds in and chases Jethro and Zeke, and they all wrestle with one another. They part for a few minutes, sniffing here and there and resting. Then Jethro walks over to Zeke, extends his paw toward Zeke’s head, and nips at his ears. Zeke gets up and jumps on Jethro’s back, bites him, and grasps him around his waist. They then fall to the ground and mouth wrestle. They chase and then roll over and play. Suki decides to jump in, and all three frolic until they’re exhausted.

For an ethologist, play is a behavior to take seriously, and it's also serious business for animals at play. Yet when I first started studying play decades ago, a number of my colleagues didn’t think so. They thought play should be tossed into a “wastebasket” because there wasn't any obvious goal or function.

On the surface, many people thought that play serves no obvious purpose. Very few people think that today. Play is improvisational and mixes a hodgepodge of behaviors from other contexts, like fighting, mating, hunting, self-defense, and so on. Dogs might growl, bite, hump, and chase in quick succession, and they might exaggerate, minimize, and interrupt these behaviors. After growling fiercely, they might bite softly, and after mounting and starting to hump, they might abruptly quit and take turns chasing. These behaviors are a kaleidoscope of the senses that helps to define play.

That’s a lot to get out of watching animals goof off and zoom around. But that’s what can happen when you observe animals closely and think carefully about what they do and why. Since play is defined by joy, it’s valid to ask: Why did play evolve—what is it good for? How do we define and recognize it? And how does it help animals survive?

After decades of studying play, I’ve learned that play is very important, and my research has led to a series of wide-ranging questions. These include: How do animals communicate that they’re playing and not doing something else, like fighting or mating? How do animals play? Does play require certain agreements to ensure cooperation, trust, and reciprocity, as well as to repair trust—such as apologizing—if something goes wrong? If so, does that mean animals have a basic sense of justice or morality? And if that’s true, then is morality an evolved trait? Does “being fair” mean being more fit in evolutionary terms? In other words, do nice guys, gals, and their genes last longest? Do the friendliest and nicest individuals survive best?

Social play is almost like school for nonhuman animals, and it's not just for fun. Play helps individuals within the group to get along, since play relies on and teaches trust, cooperation, niceness, fairness, forgiveness, and humility. Meticulous studies have shown that play fosters physical development and motor skills, it provides critical socialization, it helps develop physical life skills (like hunting and self-defense), and it develops the mind, in part by allowing animals to train for unexpected situations. Play feeds brain, body, and community, teaching young animals what they will need to do to survive in the world as well as the interpersonal skills to thrive in their own society. Play is also an important consideration for dogs that are adopted. In the United States, shelter dogs who don’t choose to play with objects are less likely to be adopted.

For a model of fair play, let’s go to the dogs. Dogs signal social play using the “play bow.” This is what Jethro does first in my field notes above: He crouches on his forelegs, his hindlegs straight and his tail wagging. With or without barking, this is how dogs say, “I want to play with you!”

The play bow both initiates play and keeps it going if there’s a break. It’s used whenever something happens that might end play. For instance, if a dog is about to do something, or just did something, that might be misinterpreted—like growling viciously and biting—the play bow says, I’m going to bite you, but it’s only in play. Or, I didn’t mean to bite so hard; let’s keep playing. So, if you don’t want to play, don’t bow.

Uncooperative play is an oxymoron. When cooperation and fairness break down, play not only stops, but it also becomes impossible. In essence, animal play appears to rely on the universal human value of the Golden Rule: Do unto others as you would have them do unto you. I summarize this as “the four golden rules of play”: (1) Ask first and communicate clearly; (2) Mind your manners; (3) Admit when you are wrong; (4) Be honest.

All in all, social play is based on a foundation of fairness, perhaps a uniquely egalitarian behavior. If we define morality as a set of social rules and expectations that neutralize differences among individuals in an effort to maintain group harmony, then that’s exactly what we find in animals when they play.

I’ve truly enjoyed watching how different patterns of animal play went from being discarded as a “wastebasket” of useless information to playing a key role in the development of ideas and theories about the evolution and development of animal morality—wild justice, as Jessica Pierce and I call it—and finding a home in areas such as human development and business ethics. And what's really exciting is that there is room for much more research on animals who frenetically zoom around here and there without a care in the world.

Bekoff, Marc: Play Signals as Punctuation: The Structure of Social Play in Canids. Behaviour, 132, 419-429, 1995; Social Communication in Canids: Evidence for the Evolution of a Stereotyped Mammalian Display. Science, 197(4308), 1097-1099, 1977; Canine Confidential: Why Dogs Do What They Do. University of Chicago Press, Chicago, 2018; The Power of Play: Dogs Just Want to Have Fun; How and Why Dogs Play Revisited: Who’s Confused?

Bekoff, Marc, and Jessica Pierce. Wild Justice: The Moral Lives of Animals. University of Chicago Press, Chicago, 2009.

Burghardt, Gordon M. The Genesis of Animal Play: Testing the Limits. Cambridge, Massachusetts, A Bradford Book, 2005.

Käufer, Mechtild. Canine Play Behavior: The Science of Dogs at Play. Doggies Publishing, 2014. (For a review of this book, see Dogs at Play: What They Do, Know, Think, and Feel.)

Palagi, E. Not just for fun! Social play as a springboard for adult social competence in human and non-human primates. Behavioral Ecology and Sociobiology 72, 90, 2018.

#4748. California has way more bugs than we thought

Published Nov 4, 2026 2:00 PM EST

It’s true that there are more insects on Earth than any other animal. They make up roughly 80 percent of the planet’s animals and include about 900,000 known species. However, those jaw-dropping numbers can make it easy to undercount our six-legged friends. Take the state of California. Over 60,000 different species of insects reside in the Golden State, and scientists have only described about two-thirds of them. A study published today in the journal Ecography details the findings, which represents a huge bump in the estimated number of insects in California.

The study is part of the California Insect Barcode Initiative (CIBI), a $6 million project to collect and identify every species of insect in the state. Multiple institutions including the California Department of Food and Agriculture, UC Berkeley, UC Riverside, San Diego Natural History Museum, the California Academy of Sciences in San Francisco, and Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County (NHM) worked together to DNA barcode over one million insect specimens.

To build the insect library, the team gathered tissue samples from museum collections and caught living insects in 72 ecoregions around the state. Ecoregions are places that have similar ecosystems as defined by the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA). They also undertook research expeditions to 454 additional locations across California, and used Malaise traps to gather the insects. Malaise traps passively capture bugs, but require a bit of work to maintain.

“This is an example of community science. Volunteers stepped forward to help with sampling by managing traps, which we would not have been able to do for continuous weekly sampling,” Giar-Ann Kung, a study co-author and NHM Entomology collections manager, said in a statement.

The study looked at Level 3 ecoregions, which include places like the Mojave Basin and Range, Southern California Mountains, and Sierra Nevada. They found that the Mojave Basin and Range have the highest insect species richness.

The team also compared parallel ecoregions and found that each one is home to its own unique mix of insect life, even if they have a similar climate and geography. While there are parallels between locations within the same ecoregion, the team found that the richness of life across California is more abundant and more delicate than previously thought. Researchers say that these results highlight the need for more aggressive conservation of California’s wild places to protect the insects living there.
